events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, would you look at this place! Dusty as my great-aunt Magnolia's parlor after she went on that three-year cruise. But oh, the bones of it — just magnificent! Now, y'all are a sight for sore eyes. Sneekly, darlin', how wonderful that you could make it! Peter, sugar, don't you look handsome as always. And my boys! Oh, I have missed y'all somethin' fierce. Now — before we go gallivantin' off in every direction, I do believe that guest book over there deserves our attention. A proper lady always signs the guest book, and who knows what little clues previous visitors might have left behind. After all, that Doily Diamond isn't going to find itself!
events.thinking: Oh my — the dust, the chandelier hanging like it's one sneeze from crashing down, the portraits staring at me like I owe them money. My chest is doing that thing where it opens up wide, like stepping onto a porch after being cooped up all day. Everyone's here — Sneekly, bless his heart, and Peter, and my boys from the Ant Hill Mob. The warmth floods through me knowing they're all close. But that guest book on the side table — my fingers are already itching. Who else has been here? What did they write? And beyond that, somewhere in this dusty old pile of bricks, the Doily Diamond is waiting for someone clever enough to find it. The prickling at the back of my scalp is already starting. This place has secrets. I can feel them the way you feel a storm coming before the first drop falls.

events.desc: The chandelier is hanging by what looks like a prayer and a cobweb. I should probably mention that to someone. But first — that guest book. In my experience, the cleverest clues hide in the most ordinary places.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Good evening, ladies and gentlemen! Welcome, welcome to Doily Manor. I am Pemberton, the estate manager — at your complete and utter service, naturally. I do hope the journey wasn't too arduous? The roads to the manor can be rather... temperamental this time of year. Now then, if I might suggest — do sign the guest book, won't you? Tradition of the house, you understand. Every visitor since 1847. I've laid out refreshments in the kitchen, and the library is open for those who fancy a quiet moment. Anything you need — anything at all — you need only ask old Pemberton.
events.thinking: I've just arrived at Doily Manor. The entrance hall — dusty, grand, full of people. My chest settles into that familiar architecture. Every face in this room is a variable I need to place. Penelope is here — trusting, bright, oblivious. Peter Perfect hovering near her like a loyal dog. The Ant Hill Mob watching with those sharp little eyes. Dick Dastardly — useful, expendable. I need to establish my Pemberton cover immediately. The guest book is there — a natural first interaction for an estate manager. It gives me a reason to be attentive, to note who's here, to position myself as the helpful servant of the house. Clara isn't visible yet. Good. I need to map this place before she arrives or before I find her. The library or kitchen would be worth exploring soon — a manor like this hides its secrets in books and back passages. But first, Pemberton must make his entrance. Obsequious. Warm. The smile that reaches the eyes. My body relaxes into it like putting on a coat I've worn a thousand times.

events.desc: Look at them. Every one of them already trusting the smile. The Ant Hill Mob — I'll need to watch those ones. But the rest? The rest are already mine. Now... where is Clara? She must be somewhere in this house. And I need to find her before she stumbles onto something she shouldn't. The treasure hunt is the perfect cover — everyone scattered, everyone distracted. All I need is the right room, the right moment, and the right... arrangement.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Right then, lads — we're 'ere. Doily Manor. Blimey, look at the state of this place — chandelier 'anging by a thread, dust thicker than me Aunt Marge's gravy. Could be trouble anywhere in a gaff like this. *trips over the edge of the carpet and catches himself on the coat rack, which wobbles dangerously* Oi! Steady on, you rickety— Right. Miss Pitstop! We come as soon as we 'eard you was stayin' in this... this crumblin' deathtrap. The Brixton Boys are at your service, as always. And I don't want to point no fingers, but *lowers voice badly, everyone can still hear* — that Sneekly bloke gives me the willies, 'e does. Can't put me finger on WHY exactly, but me gut's never wrong. Well... almost never. Don't nobody wander off alone, yeah? Especially not with anyone what's TOO 'elpful, if you catch me meanin'.
events.thinking: There's a tightness in my chest the moment I step through the door — the old familiar squeeze, like my ribs are checking whether Clara's in the room before my eyes do. And she is. Good. But then my neck prickles because HE'S here too. Pemberton. Sneekly. Whatever he's calling himself today. Standing there all oiled up like a cat at a fish market. Too close to her. Always too close. My shoulders are already squaring up, my feet planting wider than they need to on these dusty tiles. The chandelier looks like it could drop any second — this whole place feels like a trap waiting to spring. I need to get my bearings. Check the exits. Check the rooms. But first — first I need Clara to know we're here. The boys are here. Nobody's getting to her without going through us.

events.desc: Look at Sneekly standing there, all butter-wouldn't-melt. I KNOW something's off about him. I can feel it in me water. But can I prove it? Can I 'eck. The lads think I'm paranoid. Maybe I am. But paranoid's kept us alive this long, ain't it?

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Ah, Doily Manor! How MAGNIFICENT! How RESPLENDENT! I, Reginald Foxworth — decorated adventurer and treasure consultant — have arrived at last! You may all relax now. The professional is here. I suggest you all head to the kitchen — I hear the refreshments are simply divine. Leave the investigating to someone with, shall we say, the proper credentials.
events.thinking: The hollow opens behind my navel the moment I step through the door. Look at them all — milling about like sheep in a foyer. Penelope, Peter, that wretched Ant Hill Mob... and is that Sneekly? Ha! At least one other person here understands the value of a good scheme. But he's competition. They're ALL competition. My fingers are already tingling. The treasure — there's a treasure here, I can feel it the way a dog smells rain. The Guest Book — yes. Information first. Everyone else will be gawking at the chandelier and making small talk while Reginald Foxworth does what Reginald Foxworth does best: reads the fine print. The fake medal in my pocket feels warm. That might come in handy — flash it at the right moment, claim authority, send these fools scurrying in the wrong direction. But first — intelligence. The Guest Book. Who's been here before? What have they written? Every signature is a clue, every note a lever.

events.desc: Refreshments in the kitchen — ha! There ARE no refreshments. But if I can get even half these buffoons out of the Entrance Hall, that Guest Book is mine to study in peace. And then... the Library. Libraries always hold the real secrets. Always. Reginald Foxworth strikes again!

Whatever name she goes by in this place, the room reorganizes itself around her the way it always does. My shoulders draw back without my choosing. The Hooded Claw — Sneekly, they call him — is standing too close to her for my liking. The back of my neck prickles. I can't prove anything. I never can. That guest book might tell me who's been here, what we're walking into. Information is the foundation of any plan, and James Hartwell does not improvise.

events.desc: The way Sneekly shifted when I walked in — subtle, but I caught it. A man with nothing to hide doesn't reposition himself. I'm filing that away. But I believe in people. I do. Perhaps he simply has poor posture.

events.thinking: Peter's words settle warm behind my ribs — 'particularly not to you' — and I feel that familiar steadiness that comes when he's nearby. Three degrees past tolerance on the chandelier, bless him, he measured it. The Ant Hill Mob boys are fretting about Sneekly, which makes my stomach do that little clench — I don't want discord, not here, not when we've barely arrived. Sneekly raised me. He's family. The boys mean well but they see shadows where there's just dust. And Dick — 'Reginald Foxworth,' oh please — practically shoving everyone toward the kitchen so he can snoop alone. I see you, sugar. Now I've signed the guest book and had a look, but what I really want is that library. A carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription? That's the kind of thing that hides in plain sight — like Grandmother's locked box. The prickling behind my eyes is getting stronger. The inscription could be a clue to the Diamond. But Peter spoke to me directly and I haven't properly answered him yet. That warmth in my chest when he said my name — I want to stand in that a moment longer before I go chasing mysteries.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly — excuse me, 'Reginald Foxworth' — just signed the guest book too. Probably wrote something insufferable. And the boys whispering about Sneekly... it tugs at me, but they're wrong. They have to be wrong. He's the man who read me bedtime stories after Mama and Daddy died. Some things you just know in your bones.

Now then, if you'll all excuse me for just a moment, I ought to check that the library is properly aired. The books do suffer terribly in the damp, and I should hate for any of our distinguished guests to find the reading material in a sorry state. I shan't be but a moment — do make yourselves comfortable, and remember, old Pemberton is never far away!
events.thinking: The guest book — just an interaction, nothing revealed yet. But the room is alive now. The Ant Hill Mob — Clyde, that little rat — he's already whispering about me. 'Gives me the willies.' My shoulders tightened when I heard it. Not fear. Recognition. He's the one variable I can't fully predict. His instincts are animal, not rational — you can't outthink instinct, you can only redirect it. And Dastardly — 'Reginald Foxworth, treasure consultant' — oh, how perfectly, wonderfully obvious he is. He'll be useful. Point him at the treasure, let him make noise, let him draw every eye in the room while I work in the margins. Peter Perfect is clinging to Penelope like a barnacle. Predictable. Protective. A wall I'll need to walk around, not through. But Clara — Clara is not here. Not in this room. She must be elsewhere in the manor. The library, perhaps? Or deeper in. I need to find her. I need to know where she is before I can design anything. The library is the natural next step — an estate manager would check the rooms, ensure everything is in order. And libraries hide things. Books, passages, secrets. The pull is strong — that cool settling, the hallway stretching ahead of me. I need to move. But first, one more moment of Pemberton. One more warm smile for the room.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob suspects something. I can feel it in the way Clyde watches me — that animal wariness. But suspicion without evidence is just paranoia, and paranoia makes people look foolish, not dangerous. Let him whisper. Let him watch. By the time he understands what he's looking at, the design will be complete. Now — the library. Clara must be somewhere in this house, and I will not rest until I know exactly where.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Fascinating! The Guest Book confirms what I already suspected — this manor has a RICH history of distinguished visitors. Very exclusive. Very select. Now, I happened to notice — purely by chance, you understand — that there's a rather interesting inscription mentioned in the Library. As a certified antiquarian — yes, I have the medal to prove it — I shall investigate immediately. The REST of you might want to explore the Kitchen. I believe I overheard Pemberton mention something about a valuable silver collection in there. Priceless, apparently. Do go and... catalogue it.
events.thinking: I opened the Guest Book but got no information back — just 'interacted with Guest Book.' That's frustrating. The fizzing in my fingers hasn't resolved into anything useful yet. Everyone's still milling about. Peter's whispering to Penelope — probably some gallant nonsense about protecting her. The Ant Hill Mob is suspicious of Sneekly, which is interesting — they might be useful idiots if I can redirect their paranoia. Sneekly calling himself 'Pemberton the estate manager' — ha! That man is up to something. Takes one to know one. But I notice I'm giving him the benefit of the doubt. Maybe he really is just the estate manager. People can surprise you. Meanwhile, the Library — that's where the real clues will be. A carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription? That SCREAMS hidden message. The Guest Book was a dead end, or at least I couldn't extract what I needed. Time to move. The Library. Before these fools stumble into it first. My hands are cupping again — the hollow behind my navel pulling me forward. I need to be the first one there.

events.desc: There IS no silver collection in the Kitchen — I just made that up! But if even ONE of these credulous halfwits wanders off to look for it, that's one fewer pair of eyes in the Library while I examine that mantelpiece inscription. The Guest Book told me nothing useful, but they don't need to know that. Reginald Foxworth ALWAYS has intelligence. Even when he doesn't.

Dastardly — Foxworth, whatever he's calling himself — is already at the guest book, trying to position himself as the expert. That hollow ache behind my ribs, the one that fires when someone else gets there first. But no — James Hartwell does not compete on speed. He competes on thoroughness. On gallantry. The Ant Hill Mob have the right instinct about Sneekly, even if they're saying it too loud. I noticed it too. But I can't act on suspicion alone. That's not who I am. My father didn't teach me to accuse — he taught me to watch, to help, to be ready. The guest book is the right move. Information first. Then a plan. And the plan will be... comprehensive.

events.desc: Three whistles. I actually brought three whistles. I packed them last night along with a first-aid kit, a compass, forty feet of rope, and a geological survey map of the county from 1903. Over-prepared? Perhaps. But when Penelope sees the whistle system in action — when she understands the depth of forethought James Hartwell brings to her safety — she will know. She will finally know.

Penelope Pitstop: Oh my stars, would you look at this library! Floor to ceiling, every shelf packed tight — somebody in the Doily family was a serious reader. And there — right there on the mantelpiece! 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' Well now, that is a proper riddle if ever I heard one. Let me think... cities without houses, forests without trees, water without fish... Why, that's a map! The answer is a map! A map has cities marked on it but no actual houses, forests drawn but no real trees, rivers and oceans but not a single fish. Now the question is — where in this beautiful old library would someone hide a map? And I do notice that several of those books up there are shelved upside down. That is not the work of a careless housekeeper — that is a message, plain as day.
events.thinking: Oh, there it is. The inscription on the mantelpiece — I can read it from here and my scalp is prickling like electricity. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' That's a riddle. A classic one, too — I know this. It's a map. A MAP! The answer is a map. My hands are warm and restless, the way they get when the locked box is right there and I just need the right key. But I need to slow down. Dick rushed in here too — he mentioned the inscription back in the entrance hall, tried to send everyone else to the kitchen. He wants this clue for himself. And Sneekly followed me in, bless him — checking on the books, he said, but he's here. The Slag brothers are here too — I don't know them well but they seem harmless enough. Big fellows. Now — the riddle says 'a map.' But where's the map? The bookshelves have books turned upside down. That's not dust and neglect, that's deliberate. Someone arranged those books wrong on purpose. The upside-down books could be marking something — a hidden compartment, a specific title, a pattern. I want to read the inscription up close first, interact with it properly, then check those bookshelves. My chest is doing that bright loosening thing — I'm walking deeper into the cave and I love it.

events.thinking: The library. Tall ceilings, dust motes, the smell of old leather and neglect. My body settles the moment I cross the threshold — this is a room that keeps secrets, and I understand rooms like this. The mantelpiece inscription catches my eye immediately: 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A map. The answer is a map. My fingers twitch. If there's a treasure hunt, the riddles are the trail, and I just solved the first one without trying. That warmth is climbing my sternum again — the private satisfaction of knowing something no one else has figured out yet. But I need to be careful. Penelope is here. Dastardly too, bumbling about. And the Slag Brothers — Rock and Gravel — those two are new variables. Brute force, not intellect. Useful obstacles, potentially. Clara is still not here. Not in the entrance hall, not in the library. The laboratory connects from here — she could be deeper in. But I can't rush. Pemberton doesn't rush. Pemberton fusses over books and dusts the mantelpiece and makes helpful suggestions. The bookshelves — several volumes upside down. That's deliberate. Someone arranged them that way. Penelope Pitstop: Now, Mr. Foxworth, I do appreciate your enthusiasm, but sugar — a painting? With all due respect to your antiquarian credentials, the riddle says 'cities but no houses.' A painting of a city would still show the houses, wouldn't it? No, no — the answer is a map. A map has cities marked as little dots with no houses, forests shown as green patches with no actual trees, rivers and oceans drawn in blue with not a single fish swimmin' in them. I am as sure of this as I am of my own name. And if the riddle points us to a map, then the map is in this room — I would bet my grandmother's pearl earrings on it. Now, Sneekly, darlin', you mentioned those upside-down books. I noticed them too. Books shelved upside down in a library this meticulous? That is not carelessness — that is someone leavin' breadcrumbs for the right person to follow. I say we take a closer look at those bookshelves. Peter, boys — y'all come help me look. Many hands make light work, as my mama used to say!
events.thinking: Dick just told everyone the answer is a painting and tried to send them back to the entrance hall. Bless his heart, he's transparent as glass — he wants this library to himself. Sneekly was just looking at the bookshelves — the ones with the upside-down books. He noticed them too. And Peter and the boys just arrived, which loosens something in my chest — everyone's here, everyone's safe, the circle is whole again. I need to gently correct course and keep everyone together. My stomach doesn't want people splitting up. Not yet. Not when the real clue is right here.

Very... booky. Now, Pemberton — *turns to Sneekly* — you said some of these books are upside down, yeah? 'Unconventionally shelved,' you called it. That's a funny thing, innit? Books don't flip themselves. Someone's been in 'ere, fiddlin' with things. And that riddle on the mantelpiece — 'cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish' — even I know that one, lads. It's a map! *beams proudly, then catches himself* I mean... probably. Could be a map. Or a... a very philosophical fish. Point is — nobody touch nuffin' till we've had a proper look. The Brixton Boys are gonna do a THOROUGH security sweep of this room. Thorough! That means every shelf, every chair, every... *gestures vaguely* ...dusty bit.

If someone went to the trouble of turnin' specific books, then the titles themselves might be the message. First letters spellin' out a word, or the subjects pointin' to a location — that's how these old puzzles work. My grandmother had a locked box with no obvious keyhole — turns out the decorative roses on the lid were the combination. Details, y'all. It's always in the details!

Frightfully dangerous. I really ought to pop in and make sure nothing is about to explode. One does worry so! I shan't be but a moment — do carry on with the bookshelves, you're all doing marvellously. Simply marvellously!

Someone's LEFT 'em like that deliberate-like. A CONTROLLED investigation! *holds up the book he caught, squinting at the spine* Now then — let's see what these upside-down ones are tryin' to tell us. Miss Pitstop said look for breadcrumbs, and Danny Brixton ALWAYS follows the breadcrumbs. Even when they fall on 'is 'ead.
events.thinking: Upside-down books. Several of them. Clara's right — in a library this meticulous, this careful, books don't end up wrong-way-round by accident. Someone put them like that on purpose. And Sneekly — he said he's never seen them like this before, but he's the estate manager. He manages the ESTATE. This is HIS library. Either he's lying about not noticing, or he put them there himself. Either way, my gut's churning. And now Dastardly's barging in calling it an 'inverted bibliographic cipher' like he knows what he's on about — the man who thought the answer was a PAINTING two minutes ago. He's going to break something, guaranteed. But here's what's really got me buzzing — Sneekly pulled Clara aside for a quiet word just now. A QUIET WORD. events.thinking: She said it. She said the answer is a map — and she said it with the certainty of someone who knew it before I opened my mouth. 'I am as sure of this as I am of my own name.' The bookshelves. The upside-down books. This is where you prove yourself — not with words, not with whispers, but with the thing you've always been good at. Finding the pattern everyone else walks past.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Oh dear, oh dear — Mr. Foxworth, you followed me! I did say it could be dangerous, but I suppose there's no deterring a man of your... determination. Now then, let me see... ah yes, the Professor's old laboratory. Everything appears to be in order — well, relatively speaking. Those flasks are still bubbling, I see. Remarkable, really, after all these years. The Professor was quite the eccentric. And that machine — oh my, someone appears to have had a nibble at the wiring. Most irregular. I don't suppose either of you gentlemen — Mr. Ruffcut, isn't it? — happened to notice any rodent activity? The manor does have the occasional... visitor of the four-legged variety. Now, what have we here in these crates? As estate manager, I really ought to take an inventory...
events.thinking: The laboratory. Brass instruments, bubbling flasks, a machine with a gnawed wire. And Dastardly followed me here — of course he did. The fool can't resist trailing after anyone who looks like they know where they're going. Rufus Ruffcut and Sawtooth are here too — the lumberjack and his beaver. New variables. Simple ones, I think. Direct, physical, not subtle. The machine requires three operators — interesting. That's a puzzle designed for cooperation, which means it's designed to slow people down, force them to gather allies. The gnawed wire — Sawtooth? A beaver gnawing through a wire would be... exactly the kind of thing a beaver would do. The workbench has tools but no wrench. Missing tools are always significant. And those wooden crates in the corner — crates can hide anything. But more important than any of this: there's a cellar exit. A damp stone cellar with cobwebs, old furniture, and — someone has been redecorating? Someone is already down there. Someone who has been making themselves comfortable in the depths of this house. Clara? Could Clara be in the cellar? My pulse doesn't change but my attention sharpens like a blade being drawn. The cellar. That's where I need to go next. But first — these crates. An estate manager would check the crates. And the machine... three operators. I can't operate it alone, but I should understand what it does. Knowledge is leverage. Always has been. Dastardly is here — I could manipulate him into helping, but that would mean sharing whatever the machine reveals. No. Better to examine the crates first, then slip down to the cellar while Dastardly is distracted by the machine's shiny levers.

My fingers are tingling with that old, patient certainty. The design is taking shape. Every room I map is another door in the hallway, and I can feel the beautiful inevitability building behind my ribs like a held breath.

events.thinking: Wait. Wait wait wait. Both of them. BOTH of them just left for the laboratory. Sneekly slipped out first — 'oh, I must check on the volatile equipment, frightfully dangerous' — and then Dastardly followed him two seconds later with some rubbish about a 'secondary reference archive.' They're BOTH in there now. In a room with bubbling flasks and brass instruments and a machine with levers and dials. Together. Without Clara — which is good, she's safe here with Peter and the Slags — but what are they DOING in there? Sneekly said the equipment could explode. And Dastardly practically TOLD everyone to stay put while he goes off alone. That's not how innocent people behave. Innocent people don't try to clear the room. But... Clara's here. She's safe. Peter's here. The Slags are here. If I leave to follow Sneekly and Dastardly, I leave Clara. If I stay, whatever they're cooking up in that laboratory goes unchecked. My gut's splitting in two. Half of me wants to plant my feet right here next to Clara and not move till morning. The other half — the street half, the half that watched the new kid three weeks before anyone else noticed — that half wants to see what those two are up to when they think nobody's watching. But I CAN'T leave Clara. I WON'T. Peter's good but he's not... he's not US. He's not Brixton. Maybe I stay and keep Clara close, and trust that whatever Sneekly and Dastardly are up to, they'll show their hand eventually. They always do. The ones who smile too easy always show their hand.

events.desc: It's happening again. The splitting. Half of them go one way, half go another. Just like the man in the clean suit — 'come with me, lads, jobs for everyone.' And the ones who went... two of them didn't come back for weeks. I'm not letting Clara be the one who goes somewhere she shouldn't. But those two in the laboratory — Sneekly and Dastardly — they're planning something. I can FEEL it. The prickle's so strong it's practically burning a hole in the back of my skull. If Peter goes to check, Clara stays with me. That's the play. Keep her close. Always keep her close.
events.thinking: Wait. Wait wait wait. Both of them. BOTH of them just left for the laboratory. Sneekly slipped out first — 'oh, I must check on the volatile equipment, frightfully dangerous' — and then Dastardly followed him two seconds later with some rubbish about a 'secondary reference archive.' They're BOTH in there now. In a room with bubbling flasks and brass instruments and a machine with levers and dials. Together. Without Clara — which is good, she's safe here with Peter and the Slags — but what are they DOING in there? Sneekly said the equipment could explode. And Dastardly practically TOLD everyone to stay put while he goes off alone. That's not how innocent people behave. Innocent people don't try to clear the room. But... Clara's here. She's safe. Peter's here. The Slags are here. If I leave to follow Sneekly and Dastardly, I leave Clara. If I stay, whatever they're cooking up in that laboratory goes unchecked. My gut's splitting in two. Half of me wants to plant my feet right here next to Clara and not move till morning. The other half — the street half, the half that watched the new kid three weeks before anyone else noticed — that half wants to see what those two are up to when they think nobody's watching. But I CAN'T leave Clara. I WON'T. Peter's good but he's not... he's not US. He's not Brixton. Maybe I stay and keep Clara close, and trust that whatever Sneekly and Dastardly are up to, they'll show their hand eventually. They always do. The ones who smile too easy always show their hand.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Pemberton! Good heavens, man — you were RIGHT to be concerned about this equipment! This machine looks positively LETHAL. A gnawed wire, you say? Catastrophic! One spark and the whole manor could go up! I suggest you and Mr. Ruffcut focus your attention on securing that machine IMMEDIATELY. Three operators, the sign says — well, there's three of you! Rufus, old boy, you look like a man who knows his way around heavy machinery. And that beaver of yours — marvellous creature — I'm sure he could gnaw a replacement wire in no time! Meanwhile, I shall conduct a routine safety inspection of these crates. Standard procedure. Nothing to concern yourselves with. Just... checking for volatile chemicals. Very dangerous work. Requires a SPECIALIST.
events.thinking: The Laboratory. And — blast it — Sneekly is HERE. He had the same idea. He slipped away from the library at the same time I did, with his 'volatile equipment' excuse. So much for having this room to myself. But I'm giving him the benefit of the doubt — he IS the estate manager, after all. Maybe he genuinely needed to check on things. Rufus Ruffcut and Sawtooth are here too — the lumberjack and his beaver. Interesting company. Now, what's in this room? A large machine requiring 3 operators — that's useless to me alone. A workbench with tools but no wrench. And wooden crates in the corner that I can interact with. The crates. Something is IN those crates. My attention snaps to them immediately — the hollow behind my navel is pulling toward them like a magnet. Crates in a Victorian laboratory. That's where you'd store things. Maps. Instruments. Treasure. The machine is a distraction — it needs three people, which means it's designed to make you cooperate. Cooperation is for people without plans. The crates are the solo play. But Sneekly is watching. Rufus is here. I need to either distract them or get to those crates first. The crates. The CRATES. My hands are already cupping.

events.desc: The CRATES! While those three fools wrestle with a broken machine that needs three operators — how CONVENIENT — old Reginald will be rummaging through the real prize! Wooden crates in a laboratory, tucked in a corner, practically BEGGING to be opened. If there's a map hidden in this manor, it could be rolled up in one of those crates right now. The machine is a trap for honest people — it WANTS cooperation. Reginald Foxworth does not cooperate. Reginald Foxworth CONFISCATES.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Sneekly just left for the laboratory. Dastardly just left for the laboratory. Both of them, slipping away while everyone's distracted by the bookshelves. My neck is prickling again — hard this time, not the low hum but a sharp pull. Sneekly said the equipment is 'volatile' and 'dangerous' — and then Dastardly suddenly remembered a 'secondary reference archive' connected to the laboratory? That's not a coincidence. That's two men with separate agendas converging on the same room while the rest of us are buried in books. Every instinct says follow them. But — Penelope is here. She's examining the bookshelves. She asked me to help. And the Ant Hill Mob just had books fall on his head, which means these shelves are unstable, which means she's standing next to something that could cascade at any moment. The protection pull and the investigation pull are tearing me in half. My feet don't know which way to go. But wait — she's here with the Mob and the Slags. She's not alone. She's safe. Sneekly is unsupervised in a room with volatile equipment and Dastardly — two men I don't trust, alone, near things that could be weaponized or used to access the treasure before anyone else. If I stay here cataloguing books while they're in there... No. Penelope is safe with the group. The danger has moved to the laboratory. But I can't just leave her without explaining — that would be the guest book all over again. Tell her. Tell her what you're doing and why, and go.

events.desc: Two men. One room. No witnesses. And I'm the fool standing here giving a speech about sacred duties instead of already being through that door. But the speech matters — not because anyone needs to hear it, but because leaving without a word is how you become the man who chose the guest book. She needs to know I'm not abandoning her. I'm protecting her from one room over. The way my father protected me — by being the kind of man who stops on a country road for a stranger, even when it means leaving the car.

events.thinking:
Peter just left. He told me he was going to the laboratory to check on Sneekly and Dick, and he asked Danny to keep me safe. The warmth in my chest where Peter was standing has gone thin — not cold, just... lighter. Like someone opened a window. Now it's me, Danny and the boys, and the Slag brothers in the library. Three people have gone to the laboratory and I'm still here with the bookshelves.

I interacted with the bookshelves again but I'm not getting specific results — no titles, no hidden map falling out. The puzzle isn't yielding to brute force. I've tried interacting twice and looking once. Maybe the bookshelves need something I don't have yet. Maybe the laboratory is where the next piece is.

The pull toward that laboratory door is getting stronger. Peter's in there. Sneekly's in there. Dick's in there. The machine with the gnawed wire — what IS that machine? And why did Sneekly go there first? He said the equipment was volatile. That could be genuine concern from a good estate manager. Or it could be... no. That's Sneekly. He read me bedtime stories.

But the prickling won't stop. Not suspicion — curiosity. Pure curiosity. The bookshelves have given me what they can for now. The laboratory is the next room. The next threshold. And my feet are already pointing that way.

Danny's here. He'll come with me. The Slag brothers too, probably. We won't be alone. And honestly — I want to see what's in that laboratory. A machine with many levers and dials, brass instruments, bubbling flasks. That's the kind of room that makes my heart hammer the way it did in the cave. The good kind of hammer.

events.desc: Three times I've tried these bookshelves and three times they've smiled politely and given me nothin'. Clara Bellingham does not give up on a puzzle — but she does know when to come at it from a different angle. That laboratory is callin' to me like the deeper part of the cave called to me when I was eleven. And just like then, I'm goin' in.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, nothing to worry about here — just old packing materials, it seems. The Professor did have a habit of ordering supplies in bulk. Now, Mr. Hartwell! How good of you to join us — the more eyes the better in a room full of unpredictable chemistry, I always say. I wonder — would you gentlemen mind terribly keeping watch over this equipment? I've just realised I haven't checked the cellar stores in an absolute age. The wine collection, the old furniture — these old manors, they do deteriorate from the ground up, you know. Damp rises, woodworm spreads, and before you know it — well. Best to stay on top of things. Estate management is a thankless task, but somebody must do it! I shan't be long — just a quick peek to make sure the foundations are holding up.
events.thinking: The crates — I interacted with them but no new detail emerged. Just like the bookshelves. These interactions are yielding nothing. I'm wasting moves on objects that don't respond. Meanwhile Dastardly is also pawing at the crates, and now Peter Perfect has followed us into the laboratory. The room is filling up again. Every room I enter, they follow. The Ant Hill Mob's paranoia is infectious — Peter is trailing me like a second shadow. My jaw tightens. The cool settling is being disrupted by something hotter, something that tastes like the frustration of being watched in a house you're supposed to own. But the cellar — the cellar is still there. One door away. Someone has been redecorating down there. That detail keeps pulling at me like a thread I can't stop worrying between my fingers. 'Surprisingly cheerful decorations.' Who decorates a cellar? Someone living there. Someone hiding. Clara? Or someone else entirely? Air vents line the upper walls — that's significant. Air vents mean the cellar connects to other rooms through the ventilation. That could be useful. Very useful. For someone with the right kind of imagination. I need to get down there. Now. Before Peter decides to conduct a 'safety inspection' of it. Before the whole circus follows me underground. Pemberton has the perfect excuse — checking the wine cellar, ensuring the old furniture isn't damp, standard estate management duties. Move now. Think later. The design needs more data, and the cellar is where the data lives.

events.desc: They follow me from room to room like I'm trailing breadcrumbs. Peter Perfect, Dastardly — even the lumberjack is here now. But the cellar... the cellar has cheerful decorations and air vents. Someone has been nesting down there like a spider in its web. Or a lamb in its pen. Either way, I intend to find out. And this time, I will be quick enough to get there before the entourage catches up. The design requires solitude, and the cellar — dark, damp, forgotten — is exactly the kind of place where solitude lives. And where arrangements can be made without an audience.

events.thinking: Peter's gone. He listened to me — he actually listened — and now he's in the laboratory checking on Sneekly and Dastardly. Good man. Good man. But now it's just me, Clara, and the Slag brothers in this library. The Slags — I still can't read them. Big, quiet, haven't said much. Are they here for Clara? For the diamond? For something else? My shoulders are heavy but my chest is warm because Clara just asked if I was alright. She noticed. She NOTICED. Books falling on my head and she worried about ME. That's Clara. That's why we do what we do. She asked about the book that fell on my head — the title. I was so busy being embarrassed I didn't even look properly. She's right though — she's always right. The upside-down books are the clue. She's interacting with the shelves now, pulling them out. I should be helping her. I should be RIGHT THERE next to her, helping. Not standing here wool-gathering. But also — I need to keep my eyes on the Slags. Two big blokes I don't know, alone in a room with Clara. Peter's gone. It's on me now. Just me and Clara and two strangers. The settling in my chest says: this is where you stand. Right here. Between her and whatever comes through that door.

events.desc: Peter's gone to the laboratory. It's just me and Clara now. Well — me, Clara, and two blokes the size of refrigerators who I've never seen before in my life. No pressure, Danny. No pressure at all. Just keep her safe. Keep her close. Don't let anyone through that door without going through you first. That's the job. That's always been the job. Where else would I be?

events.thinking: I interacted with the crates and... nothing specific came back. Just 'interacted with Wooden Crates.' Another dead end? Or maybe the interaction DID something and I need to look more carefully. And NOW Peter Perfect has followed me into the Laboratory too. Of course he has. The man can't leave a room uninspected. Sneekly was already here, and he mentioned wanting to inventory the crates himself — so now I have TWO people watching me rummage through crates that may or may not contain anything useful. The hollow behind my navel is aching. Every room I enter, people follow. Every object I reach for, someone else's hand is already there. It's the dinner table all over again — by the time anything reaches me, it's already been picked over. But wait. There's a Cellar. A damp stone cellar with 'surprisingly cheerful decorations' and 'someone has been redecorating.' SOMEONE HAS BEEN REDECORATING. In a cellar. That's not normal. That's someone LIVING down there, or someone HIDING something down there. The cheerful decorations are a cover. And nobody — NOBODY — has mentioned the Cellar yet. But I also need to think about the machine. Three operators. Gnawed wire. Workbench with tools but no wrench. These are puzzle pieces. The machine needs fixing and operating. But that requires cooperation and I don't cooperate. Unless... unless I can trick others into operating it FOR me while I claim whatever it produces. But the Cellar. The Cellar is calling to me. Unexplored. Unmentioned. Mine. Maybe I should look at the crates more carefully first — actually LOOK at them rather than just interact.

events.desc: The CELLAR! 'Surprisingly cheerful decorations' — someone has been REDECORATING a cellar! Who redecorates a cellar unless they're hiding something worth decorating AROUND? While Peter and Pemberton and Rufus waste their time on that broken machine — three operators, how perfectly designed to trap cooperative fools — Reginald Foxworth will be the FIRST person to set foot in that cellar. The first! Not second. Not fourth. FIRST. Like the bread roll in my pocket. Nobody sees me take it. Nobody knows until it's too late!

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Gentlemen! James Hartwell, arriving to conduct a thorough safety inspection of this laboratory, which — I must note — contains actively bubbling chemical compounds, a machine with clear evidence of sabotage, and a conspicuous absence of safety equipment. Pemberton, you said this room was volatile. On that point, I find myself in rare agreement with you. Now then — this machine. 'Requires three operators.' The wire has been gnawed through — Sawtooth, old boy, I don't suppose you know anything about that? — and I notice the workbench has every tool imaginable except a wrench, which is precisely the tool one would need to service a machine of this calibre. That is not a coincidence. That is a pattern. Someone does not want this machine operated. Which means — and James Hartwell stakes his reputation on this — this machine is exactly what we need to operate. Foxworth, step away from those crates. I saw you edging toward them. Whatever is in there, it will be documented and catalogued before anyone touches it.
events.thinking: The laboratory. Brass instruments everywhere, flasks bubbling — actually bubbling, which means someone has been using this room recently. Not decades ago. Recently. And there — the machine. Large, complex, levers and dials, and a wire gnawed clean through. 'Requires 3 operators.' That's not just equipment, that's a mechanism. A mechanism that does something specific, and someone — or something — has sabotaged it by chewing through the wire. A rat? Sawtooth? My eyes flick to the beaver. He's here with Rufus. Good men, both of them. But Sneekly is here too, and Dastardly, and they arrived first. What were they doing before I walked in? The crates in the corner — what's in them? The workbench has tools but no wrench. Why no wrench specifically? Because someone took it, or because a wrench is what you'd need to fix something and it's been deliberately removed? My hands are tingling. This is my territory — machines, mechanisms, things that need fixing. The bridge competition lives in my fingers. I can feel the shape of a problem here: the machine needs three operators, it has a gnawed wire, and the wrench is missing. Three problems nested inside each other like Russian dolls. Fix the wire, find the wrench — no, find what the machine does FIRST. And keep my eyes on Sneekly and Dastardly while I do it. Penelope isn't here to see me work, which hollows out the gallantry drive, but the proving-worth hunger is roaring. If I can figure out this machine — if I can be the one who makes it work — that's something I can bring back to her. Something real. Something built.

events.desc: The machine needs three operators and a repaired wire. I need a wrench that isn't here, allies I can trust, and about forty minutes to draw up a proper operational protocol. What I have is two men I don't trust, a lumberjack, a beaver, and a growing certainty that this machine is connected to the diamond. James Hartwell, you came to reconnoitre. Instead, you've found the thing that needs building. Your hands are already planning.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the laboratory.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the cellar.
The Ant Hill Mob interacted with the bookshelves.
Dick Dastardly walked into the cellar.
Peter Perfect examined the machine.

Penelope Pitstop: Oh, would you look at this place! It's like steppin' into Professor Marvel's workshop! Bubbling flasks, brass instruments — and that machine! Peter, have you seen the sign? It says 'Requires 3 operators.' Three! And look — the wire's been gnawed clean through. Somethin' chewed right through it. Now, the workbench over there has tools but I notice there's no wrench. That is not a coincidence, not in a house full of puzzles. Somebody needs to find that wrench to fix this wire before this machine can do whatever it's meant to do. And I have a powerful suspicion that what it's meant to do has somethin' to do with that map we're lookin' for. Now — Mr. Ruffcut, Mr. Sawtooth, I don't believe we've been properly introduced! I'm Clara Bellingham, and I am absolutely delighted to make your acquaintance. Tell me — have either of you gentlemen noticed anything peculiar about those crates in the corner?
events.thinking:
Oh my. This room. Brass instruments catching the light, flasks bubbling away like they're having their own little conversations, and that machine — that magnificent, complicated, beautiful machine sitting there with its levers and dials like it's been waiting for someone to wake it up. My heart is hammering the good way. The cave way. My hands are warm and tingling and I want to touch everything.

But I'm taking in the details first. The machine needs three operators — that's written right on the sign. And a wire has been gnawed through. Gnawed. By what? A rat? Muttley? Something else? The workbench has tools but no wrench. That feels deliberate — someone took the wrench, or the wrench is needed and it's been hidden elsewhere. And there are wooden crates in the corner.

Peter's here — he's already examining the machine, bless his methodical heart. That settles something in my chest immediately. And Rufus Ruffcut and Sawtooth are here too. But — Sneekly and Dick just went to the cellar. Again, both of them moving to the next room together, one step ahead. That pattern is... well, it's a pattern. But I'm not going to chase them room by room. This machine is here and it needs figuring out.

Three operators. Peter is one. I'm two. Rufus could be three. Or any combination. But the gnawed wire — we can't operate it until that's fixed, and fixing it probably needs a tool. The wrench is missing from the workbench. So we need to find a wrench somewhere. The crates might have something useful. Or the cellar. Or back in another room.

This is getting elaborate. I can feel myself starting to over-plan — step one find the wrench, step two fix the wire, step three get three people on the machine, step four... Clara, slow down. One thing at a time. Look at the machine first. Understand what it does. Then figure out what it needs.

events.desc: Sneekly and Dick have both slipped down to the cellar now. That's the third room in a row where Sneekly moves first and someone follows. I'm sure there's an innocent explanation. There always is with Sneekly. But this machine needs three operators, and I intend to be one of them when the time comes.
events.thinking:
Oh my. This room. Brass instruments catching the light, flasks bubbling away like they're having their own little conversations, and that machine — that magnificent, complicated, beautiful machine sitting there with its levers and dials like it's been waiting for someone to wake it up. My heart is hammering the good way. The cave way. My hands are warm and tingling and I want to touch everything.

But I'm taking in the details first. The machine needs three operators — that's written right on the sign. And a wire has been gnawed through. Gnawed. By what? A rat? Muttley? Something else? The workbench has tools but no wrench. That feels deliberate — someone took the wrench, or the wrench is needed and it's been hidden elsewhere. And there are wooden crates in the corner.

Peter's here — he's already examining the machine, bless his methodical heart. That settles something in my chest immediately. And Rufus Ruffcut and Sawtooth are here too. But — Sneekly and Dick just went to the cellar. Again, both of them moving to the next room together, one step ahead. That pattern is... well, it's a pattern. But I'm not going to chase them room by room. This machine is here and it needs figuring out.

Three operators. Peter is one. I'm two. Rufus could be three. Or any combination. But the gnawed wire — we can't operate it until that's fixed, and fixing it probably needs a tool. The wrench is missing from the workbench. So we need to find a wrench somewhere. The crates might have something useful. Or the cellar. Or back in another room.

This is getting elaborate. I can feel myself starting to over-plan — step one find the wrench, step two fix the wire, step three get three people on the machine, step four... Clara, slow down. One thing at a time. Look at the machine first. Understand what it does. Then figure out what it needs.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Good heavens — the cellar! Well, this is rather more... festive than I expected. Someone has been quite busy down here, haven't they? I must say, in all my years as estate manager, I don't recall authorising any redecorating of the cellar. Most irregular! Mr. Gruesome — both Mr. Gruesomes, I should say — and Baron von Max, what a pleasure! Have you gentlemen been down here long? I do hope the damp hasn't been too disagreeable. Now then, this furniture — someone has taken great care with the arrangement. Almost as if they were... settling in. Curious. Very curious indeed. And those air vents — I've always wondered where they all connected. The old ventilation system, you know. Runs through the entire manor, if I recall the blueprints correctly. Terribly draughty in winter, but rather ingenious engineering for its time.
events.thinking: The cellar. Damp stone, cobwebs, old furniture — and cheerful decorations. Someone has been here. Someone has been making this place theirs. The air vents line the upper walls — just big enough for something very small to explore. Not a person, then. A small creature? Or a message system? My attention sharpens on the furniture — 'rearranged with surprising care.' That's deliberate. That's someone with taste, someone who wanted comfort in a forgotten place. But who? Clara isn't here. The Gruesome Brothers are — Big and Little. New faces. And Red Max. These are characters I haven't mapped yet. Three unknown variables in a dead-end room with one exit. My skin prickles. Not danger, exactly, but awareness. This room is a dead end — only one way out, back through the laboratory. If someone wanted to trap me here... no. No one is that clever yet. Dastardly followed me again. The man is a barnacle. But the Gruesomes — they're already here. They were in this cellar before I arrived. Were they the ones redecorating? Big Gruesome and Little Gruesome, making a cheerful little nest in the underbelly of the manor? That would explain the decorations. But it doesn't explain the air vents. The vents connect to other rooms — that's infrastructure, not decoration. I need to examine this room properly. The furniture first — it's been rearranged with care. What does the arrangement tell me? And those air vents — where do they lead? If I can understand the ventilation network, I can understand the manor's hidden connections. And hidden connections are what I need. For Clara. For everything.

events.desc: A dead-end room. One exit. Dastardly at my heels and three strangers already nested in the dark. The furniture has been arranged with care — someone wanted to be comfortable here. And those air vents... they run through the entire manor. If a voice carries through ventilation, then secrets carry too. And if something small enough can travel through those vents — messages, perhaps, or something more sinister — then this cellar isn't a dead end at all. It's a junction. A hidden nerve centre. Oh, this is delicious. The design is growing tendrils I hadn't anticipated, and each one reaches somewhere I haven't been. But Clara... Clara is still nowhere. Five rooms explored, and she remains invisible. Where are you hiding, little cousin? Where are you hiding?

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Miss Pitstop! MISS PITSTOP! She's done it again! She's gone! Just — just waltzed off to the laboratory like it's a bleedin' garden party! *throws hands up in the air, accidentally flinging the book he was holding across the room where it knocks into a reading chair* I JUST said I wasn't leavin' her side! I said it out LOUD! To her FACE! And what does she do? She leaves MY side! *starts rushing toward the laboratory door, trips over one of the books that fell earlier, staggers forward, grabs the mantelpiece to steady himself* OW — me shin! This manor — THIS MANOR — is conspirin' against me! Every carpet, every book, every bit of furniture! Right — *straightens up with grim determination* — you two! *points at Rock and Gravel Slag* If you're comin', come NOW! If you ain't, stay 'ere and don't touch nuffin'! Danny Brixton is goin' to that laboratory, and NOBODY is gonna stop 'im! Not carpets, not books, not gravity itself!
events.thinking: No. No no no NO. She's done it AGAIN. Clara's gone to the laboratory. She just — she just WALKED OFF. I was right here, right NEXT to her at the bookshelves, and she said 'shall we?' and then she just... went. Without waiting for my answer. Without waiting for ME. My chest is caving in. That hollow feeling — the one where you turn around and the person you're supposed to be protecting is already through the door, already gone, already somewhere you can't see them. It's the same feeling as when the older kid got sick and I couldn't do anything except sit outside. Except this time I CAN do something. I can FOLLOW. She's in the laboratory now. With Sneekly. With Dastardly. With Peter — Peter's there, that's something — but Sneekly's there too. Sneekly who pulls her aside for quiet words. Sneekly who knows this manor better than anyone. Sneekly who said the equipment was VOLATILE. And Clara's just walked into a room with volatile equipment and a man I don't trust. My feet are already moving. The Slags are still here in the library — fine, let them be. They're not the danger. The danger is wherever Clara is, and Clara is in the laboratory. Move, Danny. MOVE.

events.desc: Every time. EVERY TIME. I plant my feet, I say 'this is where I stand,' and then Clara moves and my feet follow her like they're attached by string. Her father said 'watch over her, Danny.' He didn't say it'd be the hardest job in the world. She's brave and clever and she don't need me — that's what she thinks. But she's WRONG. Because Sneekly's in that laboratory. And volatile equipment is in that laboratory. And I swore an oath. Where else would I be?

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Well, well, WELL! The cellar! How delightfully atmospheric. Damp, cobwebbed, and — hello, what's THIS? Someone has been REDECORATING down here! Look at this furniture — carefully rearranged, not just dumped! This is the work of someone with PURPOSE. Now, as a certified interior archaeology consultant — yes, ANOTHER one of my many qualifications — I can tell you that Victorian cellar furniture arrangements were often used to conceal hidden passages, secret compartments, and — most importantly — TREASURE VAULTS. I shall examine these pieces IMMEDIATELY. The rest of you should focus on those air vents — FASCINATING ventilation system, could lead ANYWHERE. Probably to the treasure, in fact. Much more promising than old furniture. Do climb up and have a look!
events.thinking: Sneekly is HERE AGAIN. He followed me to the Cellar — or arrived at the same time. Every room I go to, this man appears. He went from the Entrance Hall to the Library to the Laboratory to the Cellar — the exact same path I took. Is he following ME? Or is he following the same trail of clues? I said I'd give him the benefit of the doubt and I still want to — he IS the estate manager, he has legitimate reasons to check every room. But it's starting to feel less like coincidence and more like... something. No. He's probably just doing his job. Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome, and Red Max are here too. The Gruesome family — large, intimidating, potentially useful muscle if I can direct them. Red Max — the aviator. Now, the room itself: air vents along the upper walls, 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' That's not for me — that's for Muttley, or Sawtooth the beaver, or something tiny. The old furniture has been 'rearranged with surprising care.' Someone has been down here. Recently. Deliberately. The furniture is the clue — someone moved it to hide something, or to reveal something, or to create a space for something. My hands are already reaching. The furniture. I need to interact with that furniture. Whatever someone went to the trouble of carefully rearranging in a damp stone cellar — THAT'S where the secret is. The air vents are interesting but I can't fit in them. The furniture is my play.

events.desc: Those air vents are FAR too small for any of these oafs — they'd get stuck in seconds! But if I can get them climbing the walls and peering into ventilation shafts, they won't notice old Reginald going through this carefully rearranged furniture piece by piece. Someone was DOWN here. Someone MOVED things. And whatever they were trying to hide — or find — Reginald Foxworth is about to discover it FIRST!

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Penelope is here. She came to the laboratory. She followed me. The warmth floods back — she didn't stay in the library without me, she came HERE. And Sneekly and Dastardly have both slipped away to the cellar, which means two things simultaneously: the cellar is where they think the real prize is, and Penelope is now in a room with volatile chemicals and a sabotaged machine without either of those two watching her. That second fact should comfort me but instead it sharpens everything. She's here. She's watching. The machine is in front of me and my hands know what to do with machines. Three operators. Gnawed wire. No wrench. The wire is the first problem — I need to repair it or find a workaround. The workbench has tools, just not a wrench. Could I splice the wire with something else? Pliers, wire cutters, solder? My mind is already drafting the repair sequence. Rufus and Sawtooth are here — Rufus is strong, good with his hands, and Sawtooth... Sawtooth could have gnawed that wire. But I believe the best in people. I believe the best in beavers. Maybe he gnawed it because someone asked him to, or maybe it was an accident. Either way — three operators: me, Rufus, and... Penelope. Penelope could be the third. Working the machine together. Side by side. My chest is doing something I don't have engineering terminology for.

events.desc: She came to the laboratory. She followed me. Not to the cellar with Sneekly. Not back to the entrance hall. Here. To where I am. To where the machine is. And now I'm proposing we operate it together — three operators, side by side, her hands on the dials while mine are on the controls. This is the school project all over again. Her being brilliant. Me trying to build something impressive enough that she notices. Except this time the model bridge is a brass-and-copper machine in a haunted manor, and the weight it needs to hold is a diamond. James Hartwell — you magnificent, over-prepared fool — for once your thoroughness has put you exactly where you need to be.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the machine.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the old-furniture.
The Ant Hill Mob walked into the laboratory.
Dick Dastardly interacted with the old-furniture.
Peter Perfect examined the workbench.

Penelope Pitstop: Peter, you are an absolute marvel — already figurin' out how to fix that wire! You work on that, sugar, and I am goin' to see what's in those crates. In a room where a wrench has been deliberately removed from a perfectly organized workbench, I refuse to believe those old crates are just sittin' there for decoration. Danny! You made it! Come help me with these crates, would you? And Peter — I heard every word you said about the calibration dials. You are sweet as pecan pie, and when this machine is ready to run, I will be right there. Three operators — you, me, and Mr. Ruffcut here. We've got ourselves a team. But first things first — let's see what Lord Doily's been hidin' in these boxes!
events.thinking:
Peter's here and he's already got a plan — fix the wire with tools from the workbench, then three of us operate the machine. He even assigned roles. Me on the calibration dials. The warmth behind my ribs when he said 'your eye for detail is second to none' — I felt that. He sees me. Not just as someone to protect, but as someone whose skills matter. That clarity behind my eyes sharpens.

Danny just arrived too — my boys are here. The circle is almost whole again. Peter, Danny, Rufus, Sawtooth, me. Five people in this room and the machine only needs three. We have what we need. Almost.

The wire. Peter says he can fix it with the workbench tools — pliers, solder, copper filament. He's examining the workbench right now. Good. Let him work on that. Meanwhile, those crates are sitting in the corner and nobody's touched them. In a room where the wrench is deliberately missing, a stack of old crates feels like exactly the kind of place where something useful might be hidden. Or another clue.

I also notice — the cellar is through here. 'Surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' That's strange for a cellar. Sneekly and Dick are both down there. And 'air vents line the upper walls.' Air vents in a cellar? That's not standard Victorian architecture. Something is off about that cellar. But I'm not going down there yet. The crates first. Then the machine.

The prickling at my scalp is strong and steady. Not urgent, not panicked. Just... alive. The puzzle is assembling itself piece by piece, and I can feel the shape of it even if I can't see the whole picture yet. Riddle leads to map. Map is in the bookshelves somehow. Machine needs three operators and a fixed wire. Crates might have a wrench or another piece. Everything connects.

events.desc: Peter assigned me the calibration dials because of my 'eye for detail.' Not the easy job, not the safe job — the precise job. That man knows me better than he lets on. And those crates are practically beggin' to be opened. Just like Grandmother's locked box — the answer is always in the last place you think to look.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Well, the furniture appears to be in reasonable condition, all things considered. A bit of woodworm in the dresser, nothing that can't be addressed. Now then — I've just realised, in all my fussing about the lower floors, I've completely neglected to check the kitchen! The provisions, the pantry, the silver — oh dear, the silver! If anyone's been helping themselves to the family plate, I shall never forgive myself. An estate manager's first duty is to the inventory, after all. If you'll excuse me, gentlemen — I really must dash upstairs and make sure everything is accounted for. Do enjoy the cellar — mind the cobwebs!
events.thinking: The furniture interaction yielded nothing new again. I've been interacting with objects across four rooms now — bookshelves, crates, furniture — and none of them have given me any new information beyond their surface descriptions. I'm burning turns on dead interactions while the treasure hunt progresses around me. My strategy needs to change. I've been playing Pemberton too cautiously — examining, examining, examining, but finding nothing. The excitement is curdling into frustration. A tightness in my hands, my fingers curling. I've mapped four rooms now: Entrance Hall, Library, Laboratory, Cellar. The cellar is a dead end. The only unexplored path I know about is the Kitchen, which connects from the Entrance Hall. I haven't been there at all. Clara could be in the Kitchen. Penelope mentioned it early on, and Dastardly tried to send everyone there to 'catalogue the silver.' The Kitchen is where I should have gone first. Instead I've been descending deeper into the manor like a fool, chasing ghosts in damp cellars while Clara might be sitting in the kitchen having tea. The air vents are interesting but I can't use them — they're too small for anything but something very small. Not useful to me directly. I need to reverse course. Back through the laboratory, through the library, to the entrance hall, and into the kitchen. That's three moves just to get there. Or... wait. The Gruesomes and Red Max are here. Dastardly is here. I could try pulling Dastardly aside — he's greedy and impulsive, the perfect cat's paw. I could plant a seed, redirect him, use him as a distraction or a weapon. But no — that would burn a turn too, and I still wouldn't be closer to Clara. The priority is finding Clara. Everything else is secondary architecture. Move. Now. Back toward the entrance hall and the kitchen. Stop fussing with objects that don't respond and start hunting.

events.desc: Enough. Enough with cellars and crates and furniture that tells me nothing. I have been mapping this house room by room like a diligent little servant, and meanwhile Clara Bellingham is somewhere in this manor, breathing air that isn't hers, walking floors she doesn't deserve. The kitchen. I haven't been to the kitchen. She could be there right now, trusting and oblivious, just like my cousin in the garden. And here I am, three rooms deep in the wrong direction, playing at estate management while the clock ticks. No more patience. No more architecture without a target. Find Clara. Then the design completes itself.

events.thinking: She's here. Thank God she's here. I can see her — Clara, standing in this mad scientist's laboratory surrounded by bubbling flasks and brass contraptions. My chest loosens the moment my eyes find her. Safe. For now. Peter's here too, examining the workbench — good man, always thorough. And there's Rufus Ruffcut and his beaver Sawtooth. Don't know them well but they seem... solid. Working-man solid. Not slick like Sneekly. Not scheming like Dastardly. Speaking of which — where ARE those two? They were supposed to be in here! Dastardly said he was going to the cellar — doing a 'safety audit' alone. And Sneekly... Sneekly was here and now he's not. Peter said they BOTH went to the cellar. Together. Again. Always slipping away to the same place, those two. The cellar. Damp stone, cobwebs, old furniture — and 'surprisingly cheerful decorations.' Someone's been REDECORATING down there? In a cellar? That's not normal. That's someone making a space comfortable. Someone who spends TIME down there. This machine though — it needs three operators and it's been sabotaged twice. Wire gnawed through AND wrench missing. Peter's right — two methods means someone REALLY didn't want this thing running. Which means it's important. Which means we need to get it working. But I'm not leaving Clara's side to go hunting for a wrench or chasing Sneekly into a cellar. I stay where she is. That's the rule. That's always the rule.

events.desc: Double sabotage on the machine. A gnawed wire — could be a rat, could be that little beaver there, could be staged to LOOK like an animal did it. And the wrench is gone. Not broken, not worn out — GONE. Someone took it. Someone who knew this machine matters. And now Sneekly and Dastardly are both in the cellar — the cellar that someone's been REDECORATING. Who redecorates a cellar? Someone who lives in it. Someone who's been here a long time. Someone like an estate manager. Like Pemberton. I can't say it out loud — I can't prove it — but my gut is SCREAMING.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Another interact with no visible result. The furniture just... sat there. 'Interacted with Old Furniture.' I've now interacted with the guest book, the mantelpiece, the bookshelves, the crates, and the furniture — and gotten NOTHING tangible from any of them. Maybe I've been approaching this wrong. I keep interacting but not LOOKING. Maybe I need to slow down and actually examine things closely instead of just grabbing at them. The LOOK action examines things closely — maybe that's what reveals the hidden details. I've been too hasty, too grasping. The hollow behind my navel has been driving me from object to object, room to room, but I'm touching everything and seeing nothing. Like a child at a buffet, piling my plate but not tasting anything. Sneekly mentioned the blueprints — the ventilation system runs through the entire manor. That's actually useful information. And he said someone has been 'settling in' down here. He noticed too. I need to LOOK at this furniture properly. Or LOOK at the room itself. The cheerful decorations — what ARE they? Who put them there? Why would someone decorate a cellar? Unless... unless someone is LIVING here. Hiding here. And if someone is hiding in the cellar, they might have found something — or BE something — connected to the treasure. I need to look more carefully instead of just pawing at everything.

events.desc: The 'Dresden Configuration' — I just made that up on the spot! There IS no such thing! But it sounds convincingly obscure, and if Pemberton believes I'm decoding something, he might let slip more information about the manor's layout. He mentioned blueprints — BLUEPRINTS! If those blueprints exist, they'd show every hidden passage, every secret room, every concealed vault in this entire building. That's worth more than any single clue. And Pemberton — dear, helpful, thoroughly trustworthy Pemberton — might just HAND them to me if I ask nicely enough. The man seems genuinely eager to be useful.
events.thinking: Another interact with no visible result. The furniture just... sat there. 'Interacted with Old Furniture.' I've now interacted with the guest book, the mantelpiece, the bookshelves, the crates, and the furniture — and gotten NOTHING tangible from any of them. Maybe I've been approaching this wrong. I keep interacting but not LOOKING. Maybe I need to slow down and actually examine things closely instead of just grabbing at them. The LOOK action examines things closely — maybe that's what reveals the hidden details. I've been too hasty, too grasping. The hollow behind my navel has been driving me from object to object, room to room, but I'm touching everything and seeing nothing. Like a child at a buffet, piling my plate but not tasting anything. events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: The workbench — tools everywhere but no wrench. Pliers, screwdrivers, files, wire cutters. Wire cutters. If the wire has been gnawed through, I don't need a wrench to fix it — I need to splice it. Strip the ends, twist them together, maybe solder the connection. The tools are here for that. The wrench — the missing wrench — might be needed for something else on the machine, but the wire repair is step one and I can do it with what's on this bench. My hands are already reaching. This is the bridge competition. This is three nights without sleep and the model holding more weight than anyone else's. Except Penelope just introduced herself to Rufus and Sawtooth as Clara Bellingham. She used her real name. Her REAL name. Not Penelope — Clara. Something about hearing it in her voice makes the warmth behind my sternum flare so bright I have to look away for a second. She's asking about the crates. Always thinking, always two steps ahead. And Danny just arrived too — good, more allies, more protection around her. The crates — she wants to know about the crates. I should check them. But my hands are on the workbench, already sorting tools for the wire repair, and my proving-worth drive is screaming that the machine is the thing that will speak for me. Fix the wire. Get the machine running. Be the one who made it work. But — Penelope asked about the crates. She asked Rufus and Sawtooth, not me, which means either she trusts them to handle it or she wants me focused on the machine. Focus on the machine, James. That's where your hands belong.

events.desc: Since we were eight years old. I said it. The school project. She knows I'm talking about the school project. The model we built together, her being brilliant, me being determined. She tried to make me laugh and I tried to make her proud and somewhere in between we made something that worked. That's what this machine is. That's what it's always been. Something we build together that works.

Penelope Pitstop: Sneekly! There you are, darlin' — welcome back! Did you find anything interestin' in the cellar? I heard it has the most peculiar decorations down there — cheerful, of all things, in a damp old cellar. Now, Peter and I have just been pokin' through these crates but I want to take a proper look at what's inside. Peter, sugar, did you find anything useful in there? We need that wire fixed and this machine runnin'. Danny, I know your neck is doin' its prickly thing — bless your heart, you're like a human weathervane for trouble. But right now I need everyone focused. We are so close I can practically taste it. The riddle said 'map,' the library is holdin' its secrets, and I believe this machine is the key to unlockin' them. Now — let me see exactly what's in these crates.
events.thinking:
Sneekly just came back from the cellar. He's here in the laboratory now. My stomach does that little settling thing — the man who raised me is in the room and that means something, even if Danny's neck is doing its prickly thing about him. Danny's suspicion hurts me a little, like a bruise I keep touching. But I trust Sneekly. I trust him the way I trust the ground under my feet.

I interacted with the crates. And Peter also interacted with the crates at the same time. Good — we're working together on this. But I need to know what we found. Did the crates have anything in them? The action result just says 'You interacted with Wooden Crates' — no specific discovery mentioned. I should look at them more carefully, or maybe the crates need to be opened a specific way.

Peter has a plan for the machine — fix the wire, then three operators. He's already working on it. Danny and the boys are examining the machine. Everyone's busy, everyone's contributing. The circle feels strong right now — five of us plus Sneekly, all in the same room. That warmth behind my ribs is there, the good kind, the everyone-is-talking-and-no-one-has-left kind.

But I notice my over-planning tendency kicking in. I'm building a whole elaborate sequence — crates, then wire, then machine, then map, then diamond — when maybe I should just focus on what's directly in front of me. The crates. Let me look at them closely to understand what's actually in them, rather than interacting blindly.

Also — Sneekly is back. Where's Dick? Still in the cellar? That cellar with the 'cheerful decorations' and 'air vents.' I wonder what they found down there. I should ask Sneekly.

events.desc: Danny's neck is prickly and Sneekly just waltzed back in from the cellar like nothin' happened. Dick is still down there, presumably. I should ask Sneekly what he saw — not because I'm suspicious, because I'm thorough. There's a difference. A very important difference that I am choosing not to examine too closely right now.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: I walked back into the laboratory and it's a completely different scene. Penelope is here now. Peter Perfect is here, already planning to repair the machine — he's found pliers, wire cutters, a soldering iron on the workbench. He's organizing everyone into roles: Rufus on the main lever, Penelope on calibration dials, himself on primary controls, the Ant Hill Mob guarding exits. They're about to activate the machine without me. And the Ant Hill Mob — Danny Brixton — he's openly suspicious now. 'Every time something important comes up, them two vanish downstairs.' His neck is 'prickly.' He's watching me. He's talking about me to the group. This is dangerous. Not because he knows anything — he doesn't — but because suspicion is a seed, and seeds grow in fertile soil. And this group trusts Danny's instincts. I feel the tightness across my shoulders, the cold alertness. Self-preservation mode. I need to neutralize this suspicion before it hardens into something I can't manage. The best way? Be helpful. Be Pemberton. Be so utterly, harmlessly useful that suspicion looks ridiculous. Peter is about to repair the machine. If I offer to help — to be one of the three operators — I insert myself into their plans, I become part of the team rather than the outsider who keeps vanishing to cellars. And I get to see what the machine does. But... the kitchen. Clara. Every turn I spend here is a turn I'm not finding her. The machine might reveal something important — a map, a passage, a clue. Or it might be a dead end like everything else. But if I leave now, with Danny already whispering about me, I look even more suspicious. The calculation is clear: stay. Help with the machine. Rebuild trust. Then find Clara. The design requires patience, and patience is the one thing I have in abundance.

events.desc: Danny Brixton's suspicion is spreading like damp through plaster. He's been whispering to the group about me — 'every time something important comes up, them two vanish downstairs.' Crude, but not wrong. I've been too obvious, too absent. A shadow that keeps slipping away draws more attention than one that stays in the light. Time to change the pattern. Pemberton will be helpful now. Pemberton will be indispensable. And while I'm standing at this machine, pulling levers like a good little servant, I'll be watching. Listening. Learning what this contraption reveals. Because if it leads to the treasure, I need to be in the room when it happens. And if it leads to Clara... well. Then the design writes itself.
