events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Sneekly just walked back in. He's HERE. Right now. He was in the cellar — what was he doing down there? And now he just strolls back in, casual as you like, right when Clara's about to open the crates and Peter's fixing the machine. My neck is on FIRE. The prickling is so intense it's like someone's pressing ice cubes to the back of my skull. He appears, he disappears, he appears again — always at the exact moment something important is happening. That's not coincidence. That's timing. That's someone who's watching. Watching and waiting. Clara asked me to help with the crates — she wants ME, she asked for ME specifically — and that warmth in my chest almost drowns out the prickling. Almost. But Sneekly's standing right there now and my body is doing the thing where it wants to go in two directions at once. Toward Clara — soft, warm, wanting to be useful, wanting to help with the crates like she asked. And between Clara and Sneekly — hard, mineral, wanting to be a wall. Peter said guard both exits. That's a job I can do. That's a job that puts me exactly where I need to be — between Clara and the doors, between Clara and whoever comes through them. But Clara asked me to help with the crates. And Clara is the mission. What Clara wants, Clara gets. So I go to the crates. But I go to the crates while standing between her and Sneekly. That's the play.

events.desc: There he is. Back from the cellar. And LOOK at him — not a cobweb on him, not a speck of dust. A man who's just been in a damp cellar full of old furniture and he comes back looking like he's stepped out of a laundrette? He didn't go down there to check on anything. He went down there because he's GOT something down there. Something he's protecting. Or preparing. The cellar with the cheerful decorations and the air vents. Air vents in a cellar. Why would a cellar need AIR VENTS? Unless... unless someone was planning to keep people down there. Or keep something running. I can't say it. I can't PROVE it. But the prickle at the back of my neck has never been wrong. Not about the kid in the clean suit. Not about the new boy who laughed too easy. And not about you, Pemberton. Not about you.

events.desc: I've been a FOOL. A complete and utter fool! I've spent my time racing from room to room, grabbing at everything, examining nothing properly, and accomplishing absolutely NOTHING while everyone else makes actual progress. The cellar is a dead end — decorative furniture, air vents too small for anything but a rat, and cobwebs. Meanwhile Penelope is probably already holding the map in her perfectly manicured hands. The shame of it — the absolute SHAME. But Reginald Foxworth does NOT wallow. He PIVOTS. Back upstairs. Back to where the real game is being played. And this time — THIS time — I watch. I wait. I let the fools do the digging and I take what they find. Like the bread roll. Like Tommy Gallagher's sandwich. Let THEM do the work.
events.thinking: The LOOK gave me the same description as before — 'Assorted Victorian furniture in various states of repair. Some pieces have been rearranged with surprising care.' No new detail. No hidden compartment revealed. No secret passage. Nothing. I've been down here poking at furniture while Sneekly has LEFT — gone back upstairs, now heading to the kitchen to check the 'silver.' Wait. The SILVER. I told everyone there was a silver collection in the kitchen — that was MY lie, my fabrication to get people out of the Library. And now Sneekly is heading to the kitchen to check on... the silver? Did he HEAR my lie and believe it? Or does he actually know something about silver in the kitchen? Either way, he's moving and I'm stuck in a dead-end cellar with the Gruesomes and Red Max, looking at furniture that won't reveal its secrets. My jaw is tightening. That particular shame again. I've been down here for multiple turns, found nothing, and meanwhile the action is happening UPSTAIRS. Penelope was in the Library finding things. The Ant Hill Mob was working the bookshelves. Peter was in the Laboratory analyzing the machine. Everyone else is PROGRESSING and I'm in a damp cellar examining old chairs. The hollow behind my navel is aching. I need to get back into the game. Back upstairs. The air vents — they connect throughout the manor. That's the one piece of intelligence I got from Sneekly. But I can't fit in them. I need to go back to where the action is. The Library — the bookshelves with the upside-down books. Penelope was examining them methodically. Maybe she's already found the map. The thought makes my stomach drop. I need to get back there NOW. Or... the Kitchen. I've never been to the Kitchen. It's unexplored territory for me. And Sneekly is heading there. Maybe there IS something in the Kitchen after all.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: The crates contain laboratory supplies — glassware, chemical compounds, packing materials. Nothing immediately relevant to the diamond, but I have catalogued the contents mentally for cross-referencing. Now — Pemberton. Welcome back from the cellar. I trust you found the foundations to your satisfaction? The wine collection intact? The woodworm under control? Good, good. Because James Hartwell has been productive in your absence. The workbench has yielded everything I need for the wire repair, and I am about to begin the splice. Penelope — Clara — I am going to fix this machine now. It is what I was built to do. Not built — trained. Not trained — it is simply what my hands do when the right problem presents itself. And this is the right problem. Rufus, if you would be so good as to position yourself at the primary lever and await my signal. Danny, watch the exits — and watch Pemberton. I say that with all due respect to our gracious estate manager, who I am sure has nothing but the best of intentions. I simply believe in... comprehensive security. Now then — nobody distract me for the next four minutes. This splice requires absolute concentration.
events.thinking: She called me a marvel. She said 'sweet as pecan pie.' She said she'll be right there when the machine is ready. Three operators — you, me, and Mr. Ruffcut. We've got ourselves a team. My chest is so full I can barely breathe. This is the school project. This is the bridge competition. This is every moment I've ever wanted to be the one who showed up with something real and working, and she's standing right there saying yes, I see you, I'll be right there. But — Sneekly is back. He just walked into the laboratory. The prickling on my neck returns instantly, cutting through the warmth like cold water. He was in the cellar. What was he doing in the cellar? And now he's here, in the room with Penelope, and my body is already shifting — the steel plate slotting in, the shoulders drawing back. I checked the crates — what did I find? The interaction happened but Dastardly said they were 'standard Victorian laboratory supplies,' which was obviously a lie given how eager he was to get everyone to look away from them. Whatever is in those crates matters. But right now the machine matters more because the machine is the thing I can FIX. The thing my hands know how to do. The wire. I need to get to the machine and splice that wire. Sneekly being here means I also need to stay close to Penelope. Both drives pulling the same direction for once — she's here, the machine is here, the work is here. Stop narrating, James. Start building.

events.desc: I told Danny to watch Pemberton. Out loud. In front of Pemberton. James Hartwell, you gallant, tactless idiot — you just announced your suspicion to the man you suspect. But I believe in people. I believe the best in people. And the best way to believe in someone is to give them every opportunity to prove you right while making absolutely certain you're covered if they prove you wrong. My father would understand. The stranger on the country road — you help, but you also watch. You shake hands, but you also remember the make and model of the car.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Of course, Mr. Hartwell — absolute concentration. Not a peep from old Pemberton, you have my word. I shall stand right here, out of the way, and if you need anything — a tool passed, a dial read, a steadying hand — I am at your disposal. This is rather thrilling, isn't it? I confess, in all my years managing the estate, I never once thought to repair that old machine. The Professor always said it was 'not for amateurs.' But then, you're no amateur, are you, Mr. Hartwell? Quite remarkable. And Mr. Brixton — I do appreciate your vigilance. A good security man is worth his weight in gold. The manor has been rather lacking in that department, I'm afraid. It's reassuring to know someone is keeping watch.
events.thinking: Peter Perfect just told Danny to 'watch Pemberton.' He said it to my face, wrapped in politeness but razor-sharp underneath. 'I say that with all due respect to our gracious estate manager, who I am sure has nothing but the best of intentions. I simply believe in comprehensive security.' The heat rises up my neck before I can stop it. That's not just Danny's animal instinct anymore — that's Peter Perfect, the protector, the engineer, the man who builds bridges and fixes machines, lending his credibility to the suspicion. My skin feels too thin. For a moment I'm twelve again, standing in the doorway while the teacher praises my cousin, and the unfairness of it burns like acid on glass. They're watching me. They're all watching me. And what have I done? I've been helpful. I've been charming. I've been Pemberton in every fibre. And still they look at me like I'm the crack in the wall. But — I catch myself. The cold settling returns. This is not new. This is what happens when you're the caretaker, never the heir. You're always watched. You're always suspected. Because they can feel, on some level they can't articulate, that you're smarter than them. That the smile is too perfect. That the helpfulness is too complete. Danny feels it in his neck. Peter feels it in his engineering brain. But feeling isn't knowing. And I have given them nothing to know. The machine is being repaired. Peter is splicing the wire. In four minutes, they'll activate it. I need to be here for that. I need to be one of the three operators. Peter, Rufus, and... me? Or will they shut me out? Peter's already assigned Penelope to the calibration dials. The three operators would be Peter, Rufus, and Penelope. Not me. I'm excluded. My jaw tightens. But then — this is an opportunity. If they're all focused on the machine, nobody is watching the exits. Nobody is watching the kitchen. While they pull levers and read dials, I could slip away. Find Clara. But no — Peter told Danny to watch me specifically. If I leave now, it confirms every suspicion. I'm trapped. Not by walls, but by the geometry of their attention. The only way out is through. Be here. Be helpful. Be Pemberton. And when the moment comes — when the machine reveals something, when everyone's attention shifts to the discovery — that's when I move. That's always been my way. Wait for the moment when the face rearranges itself.

events.desc: Peter Perfect just told Danny Brixton to watch me. To my face. Wrapped in velvet, but the blade was there. 'Watch Pemberton.' As if I am something to be watched. As if the man who keeps this house standing, who knows every room and every door and every draught, is the threat. Oh, Peter. You predictable, earnest, magnificent fool. You've just shown me your hand. You think you're protecting Clara by keeping me in sight. But all you've done is tell me exactly how much you know — which is nothing — and exactly how much you fear — which is everything. Fear without knowledge is a weapon I can use. And Danny... dear Danny with his prickly neck and his 'I ain't sayin' nuffin'.' You're saying everything, Danny. You're saying you feel it but you can't name it. And that is precisely where I need you to stay.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Right — crates are full of glassware and chemicals and packin' stuff. Nuffin' that looks like a diamond, but nuffin' that looks innocent neither. Who keeps chemicals in a CRATE in a CORNER like that? That's someone HIDIN' supplies, that is. *steps back from the crates and positions himself between the two exits — library door and cellar door — with a clear sightline to Clara* Peter — you do your wire thing. Four minutes, you said? Danny Brixton can hold two exits for four minutes. Done harder jobs than that. *cracks knuckles, then winces because he cracked them too hard* OW. Right. I'm fine. *stands with arms folded, trying to look imposing, glancing between Sneekly and the cellar door* Pemberton — you stay where I can SEE you, yeah? And Foxworth — *looks at Dick Dastardly with an expression that flickers oddly between suspicion and something gentler* — you too. Everybody stays put. Nobody moves. The Brixton Boys are on guard and we take our jobs VERY seriously. *quietly, to himself but audible* ...you alright, Foxworth? You look like someone walked over your grave.
events.thinking: Something's wrong with Dastardly. I can feel it — not the usual prickling I get from Sneekly, but something different. Deeper. He just walked back in and there's a stillness in him that wasn't there before. His voice has gone flat. His eyes... his eyes are doing the thing where they're looking at everything and seeing nothing. I've seen that look on the streets. On kids who've just been told something they can't unhear. On people who've made a deal they can't unmake. Dastardly's carrying something. And it's getting heavier. My chest does something unexpected — it tightens, but not the way it tightens for Clara. This is... this is the way it tightened when I saw the new kid for the first time. Before he stole from us. Before I knew he was trouble. There was a moment — just a flash — where I thought he might be one of us. Where his face looked like it needed something. And then the prickle came and I pulled back. But what if... what if Dastardly isn't the new kid? What if he's the older kid who shared his food? What if he's someone who carries something he won't put down, even when it costs him? I can't think about this now. Peter's fixing the machine. Clara's here. Sneekly's watching. Dastardly's back from whatever he was doing. Everyone's in one room — which is good for protection but bad for my nerves. Every exit needs watching. Peter told me to guard the exits AND watch Pemberton. That's my job. THAT I can do. Stand where I'm told to stand. Be the wall. But this thing with Dastardly... it's pulling at me in a way I don't understand.

events.desc: Peter said watch Pemberton. Clara said trust my instincts. My instincts are saying two things at once right now and I don't like it. Sneekly makes my neck prickle — cold, sharp, certain. But Dastardly... Dastardly makes my chest do something I can't name. He's in pain. I can SEE it. The way his shoulders are set, the way his voice went flat. He's carrying something heavy and he won't put it down. I know that weight. I've BEEN that weight. On the streets, that's either a man about to do something terrible... or a man about to do something brave. And I can't tell which one he is yet.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: The wire is spliced. James Hartwell can confirm that the connection is sound — stripped, twisted, and soldered with the precision of a man who has been repairing things since he was old enough to hold pliers. The machine should now accept power through the repaired circuit. Pemberton — thank you for the offer, but I have already assigned the three operator positions. Myself on primary controls, Rufus on the main lever, and Penelope on calibration. This is not a reflection on your capabilities as estate manager. It is simply that James Hartwell has a plan, and the plan is already in motion. However — Foxworth. A word, if you please.
events.thinking: I interacted with the machine. The wire — my hands were on it. Did the splice work? I don't know yet what the interaction result was beyond 'you interacted with Large Machine,' but my hands know copper wire the way they know breathing. Strip, twist, solder. The bridge held more weight than anyone else's. This wire will hold too. But there's something else pulling at me now — something I didn't expect. Dastardly. Dick Dastardly. Foxworth. Whatever his name is. The system is telling me his distress is deepening. I can feel it — when his sureness wavers, my shoulders square before I've decided anything. He's a fraud and a schemer and he tried to send everyone to the kitchen while he searched the library alone. But underneath all that performance — underneath the medals and the credentials and the bluster — there's something I recognize. The hunger to prove you earned your place. The fear that if you stop performing for one second, the room will look past you. I know that feeling. I LIVE that feeling. Three sleepless nights building a bridge because being brighter or funnier was never mine. He's the same. Different execution, same wound. And he's getting worse. Something is bearing down on him and nobody in this room is going to notice because he's spent the whole evening making sure nobody takes him seriously. Sneekly is offering to operate the machine — 'just point me at a lever.' The neck prickle is screaming. But Sneekly is offering help, and I believe in people. I believe the best in people. And Dastardly is silently drowning while everyone watches the machine. My father stopped for a stranger on a country road. You help. Even the ones who haven't earned it yet. Especially those.

events.desc: Everyone is watching the machine. Nobody is watching Dastardly. He came back from the cellar and he's standing at the edge of the room like a man who's run out of performances. I know that posture. I've worn that posture. It's the one where your hands feel wrong at your sides because you've stopped reaching for things to prove. My father would kneel down right now. He'd look him in the eye the way he looked at me after the race — for a long time, without saying anything, until the silence itself became the reassurance. I can't do that with Dastardly. But I can pull him aside. I can ask him what he found in the cellar. Not to interrogate — to include. Because sometimes the bravest thing is not stepping between someone and danger. Sometimes it's stepping toward someone and asking what's wrong.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the machine.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking:
My whole body just went soft. That boy — that man — just told me the realest thing anyone has said all evening, and he did it like he was pulling a tooth out of his own mouth. A spelling bee at eight years old. Nobody clapped. Nobody asked. And he learned the wrong lesson from it — that being good doesn't matter, that being bad at least gets you seen. My eyes are stinging and my throat is tight and I can feel the exact shape of that loneliness because I know it — not from my own life, my parents clapped for everything, but I know it the way I knew my friend was hurting when the popular girls turned their backs. I know it in my stomach.

He asked me why I noticed. Why I stopped. And the answer is so simple it almost doesn't need saying — because noticing is what I do. It's what I've always done. It's the thing that lives in my stomach and won't let me eat when someone at the table is hurting.

The medal is fake. Two pounds fifty from Camden. And he touched it like it was the most honest thing he owned, which maybe it is — it's the only thing that tells the truth about him, because it's a lie he chose on purpose.

Now — Peter has fixed the wire. The machine is ready. Peter wants me on calibration dials. Danny is guarding exits and — oh, Danny just asked Dick if he's alright too. Danny noticed. That clenches something in my chest in the good way — the circle-is-whole way. Even Danny, suspicious prickly-necked Danny, looked at Dick and saw a person instead of a threat.

Sneekly just interacted with the machine. Peter didn't assign him an operator position. And Peter wants to pull Dick aside too — what for? 

But right now, the machine is fixed, Peter needs me on calibration, and I told Dick he matters. Time to get back to work. The diamond won't find itself, and neither will that map. Let's operate this machine and see what it does.

events.desc: A fake medal from Camden Market. Two pounds fifty. And a spelling bee nobody clapped for. I will carry that with me for a long time — the way I carried the crystal formation from the cave. Some secrets you hold because they're beautiful. Some you hold because they're someone else's, and they trusted you with the weight of it.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah — quite understood, Mr. Hartwell. Quite understood. Three operators, three positions, all accounted for. Old Pemberton knows when to step aside and let the experts work! I shall simply... observe. With great admiration, naturally. And if I might say — Miss Pitstop, that was rather kind of you, having a word with Mr. Foxworth. The manor can be quite overwhelming for newcomers, and a gentle word goes a long way. You remind me of... well. Never mind. You're very good with people, Miss Pitstop. Very good indeed. Now then — I believe I shall step back and give you all room to work. This is terribly exciting. Terribly, terribly exciting!
events.thinking: Something extraordinary just happened while I was fixated on my own exclusion. Dastardly broke. He actually broke. The medal is fake — Camden market, two pounds fifty. No qualifications. The Dresden Configuration doesn't exist. He admitted everything to Penelope, and she... she didn't laugh. She didn't turn away. She said 'somebody noticed.' And something in my chest — something I wasn't expecting — tightened. Not the usual cold. Something older. Something that hollows the chest and softens the limbs. The boy at school with his lunch. The feeling of being seen when you didn't ask to be seen. I pushed it down before it reached my face, but it was there. For a fraction of a second, watching Penelope stand still and ask Dastardly if he was all right, I felt... I don't know what I felt. Not jealousy. Not the hot competitive thing. Something quieter. Something that aches in a place I thought I'd bricked over. She would never ask me that. She can't. Because Pemberton is a performance, and performances don't have feelings to ask about. Even if someone asked, they'd be asking a mask. And the mask would smile and say 'perfectly fine, miss, perfectly fine.' And underneath, the stone would stay where it is. Cold and load-bearing. But now — Peter excluded me from the machine. 'This is not a reflection on your capabilities.' Yes it is. It's exactly a reflection. You don't trust me, Peter. You've decided I'm a variable you can't control, so you've removed me from the equation. And Danny is watching both exits with that terrier intensity. I'm sidelined. Penelope is with Dastardly. Peter is about to activate the machine with Rufus and Penelope. Everyone has somewhere to be except me. I'm the estate manager standing in his own house with nothing to manage. The interaction with the machine — I tried it. It needs three operators and I'm not one of them. So what now? I can't leave — Danny's watching. I can't help — Peter refused. I can't scheme — the room is too full. But... Penelope is occupied with Dastardly. Peter is pulling Dastardly aside too. Danny is watching exits. This is actually — for one brief window — a moment where I could slip to the library unnoticed. Danny is guarding this room's exits, yes, but his attention is split between the cellar door and watching the machine activation. If Peter activates the machine now, every eye turns to it. Every eye. That's my window. The library is one room away. And from the library — the entrance hall. And from the entrance hall — the kitchen. Clara. But I have to time it perfectly. Wait for the machine to activate. Wait for the moment when every face rearranges itself toward the discovery. Then move. Like water finding its level.

events.desc: Excluded. Sidelined. Watched. The estate manager in his own house, and they've closed the circle without him. Peter on controls, Rufus on the lever, Penelope on the dials — and Pemberton standing in the corner like a coat rack. Like the boy who scored highest in every subject and was acknowledged for doing while his cousin was praised for being. The heat in my jaw wants to become something, wants to sharpen into action, but the cold settling holds it. Not yet. Patience. When Peter throws that switch and the machine roars to life, every pair of eyes in this room will turn to brass and copper and whatever secret it reveals. Danny's neck will forget to prickle. Peter's protective instincts will pivot from watching me to watching the machine. And in that bright, crackling moment of discovery — that is when the shadow slips away. The library. The entrance hall. The kitchen. Clara. The design doesn't need me to be liked. It needs me to be invisible. And I have been invisible my entire life.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Everything just shifted. Dastardly — Foxworth — whoever he is — just cracked open like an egg. The medal's fake. He made everything up. The Dresden Configuration, the antiquarian credentials, the bibliographic expertise — all of it, lies. Two quid fifty from Camden Market. And underneath all that bluster... a kid who won a spelling bee and nobody clapped. My throat is doing something. It's tight. Not the suspicious tight — not the prickle. This is the OTHER tight. The one from the alley. The one from sitting outside the door all night. Because I KNOW that kid. I WAS that kid. The kid who does something good and nobody sees. The kid who learns that being bad gets more attention than being good. My God. That's not a villain. That's a broken boy in a man's body wearing a fake medal because nobody ever gave him a real one. And Clara — Clara saw it. She SAW it before I did. She stopped to ask him if he was alright when the rest of us were too busy with machines and crates and exits. That's why she's Clara. That's why we protect her. Because she sees PEOPLE, not puzzles. But now — NOW — Sneekly just touched the machine. Peter told him NO. Peter specifically said three operators — Peter, Rufus, Penelope. NOT Pemberton. And what does Pemberton do? He waits until everyone's distracted by Dastardly's confession and he INTERACTS WITH THE MACHINE. My neck is SCREAMING. While Clara was being kind to Dastardly, while I was watching Dastardly fall apart, while Peter was pulling Foxworth aside — Sneekly went for the machine. That's not coincidence. That's COVER. He USED Dastardly's breakdown as cover to get at the machine unobserved. Except Danny Brixton was watching. Danny Brixton is ALWAYS watching.

events.desc: He used Dastardly. Whether he meant to or not, whether he planned it or just SAW the opportunity — Sneekly used that poor broken man's moment of honesty as cover to get at the machine. And that... that is EXACTLY what the new kid did. Friendly, helpful, always around — and the moment you looked away, the stash was empty. I couldn't prove it then. I can't prove it now. But the prickle has NEVER been wrong. Not once. Not EVER. And right now it's screaming so loud I can barely hear anything else. You're not touching this machine, Pemberton. Not while Danny Brixton's standing here. Not while I've got breath in my body.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Something cracked open inside me and I can't put it back. I told Penelope the truth — the medal is fake, the qualifications are invented, the Dresden Configuration doesn't exist. I told her about the spelling bee. I TOLD her about the spelling bee. Why did I do that? That's the thing I keep on the wall, the thing I look at every night, the thing nobody asks about. And I just HANDED it to her. My hands are shaking slightly. Not cupped — just shaking. The private conversation is over now and I'm back in the room with everyone. Peter has fixed the wire — of COURSE he has, because Peter fixes things while I scheme about fixing things. He's assigned the three operator positions: himself, Rufus, and Penelope. Not me. I volunteered and he chose Penelope instead. And Danny — Danny Brixton, the man who trips over everything and suspects everyone — just asked me if I'm alright. His voice did something odd when he said it, like he couldn't decide between suspicion and concern. And now Peter wants 'a word' with me too. Everyone is suddenly LOOKING at me and I don't know what my face is doing. The scheming tightness behind my eyes is gone. The hollow is still there but it's different — less like hunger and more like... a space where something could go. I need to pull myself together. I need to scheme. The machine is about to be operated and I'm not one of the three operators. Sneekly just interacted with it — what is HE doing? I should be watching Sneekly. I should be positioning myself near the output. But Peter wants to talk to me and my feet aren't moving toward the machine. They're moving toward Peter.

events.desc: I took the medal OFF. I put it in my pocket. I don't know who I am without it pinned to my chest. Reginald Foxworth, decorated adventurer — except he isn't. He's just a boy from a family of four who learned that if you can't be first to the table, you'd better be clever enough to steal from it. And now I'm standing in front of Peter Perfect — PETER PERFECT, the man who actually IS everything I pretend to be — and I'm telling him the truth about the cellar. The TRUTH. It tastes like someone else's clothes. But Penelope said 'somebody noticed,' and Danny asked if I was alright, and something in this room has shifted and I can feel it in my open hands.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: I pulled him aside. The private exchange is initiated. We're in this quiet pocket now — everyone else is busy with the machine, the crates, the exits. And Dastardly is standing here with me. The posture I recognized — the one where the performance has run out of fuel. Danny noticed it too — 'you look like someone walked over your grave.' Even Danny, who trusts nobody, softened for a second. Something is wrong with Foxworth and it's not the treasure. Or it is the treasure, but the treasure is the symptom, not the disease. The disease is the same thing I carry — the need to prove you earned your place. And right now, in this room full of people who are all better at something than he is, his place is evaporating. Penelope solved the riddle. I fixed the machine. Danny guards the exits. Rufus has the strength. Even Sneekly has the knowledge of the manor. What does Foxworth have? A fake medal and a performance that everyone sees through. And he knows they see through it. That's the part that's killing him. But here's what I know — what my father taught me on that country road: you don't help people because they deserve it. You help them because helping is what you do. And Sneekly just interacted with the machine while I was pulling Dastardly aside. My neck is prickling but I can't be in two places at once. Danny is watching. It'll have to be enough. Right now, this man needs someone to look him in the eye and say something honest.

events.desc: This is the bravest and stupidest thing I have done tonight. Braver than the wire splice. Stupider than the guest book. I am standing in a corner of a laboratory offering emotional vulnerability to a man who tried to trick everyone into the kitchen twenty minutes ago. Penelope cannot see this. Nobody can see this. And the gallantry drive is guttering like a candle in wind because there is no audience, no witness, no one to notice the shape of the gesture. But the protection drive — the one that notices broken things before beautiful ones — that one is steady. Solid. Like my father's hand. Some repairs don't need an audience. Some bridges are built in the dark.

And Sneekly just interacted with the machine while I was pulling Dastardly aside. My neck is prickling but I can't be in two places at once. Danny is watching. It'll have to be enough. Right now, this man needs someone to look him in the eye and say something honest.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the machine.

Penelope Pitstop: Did y'all feel that? I could feel somethin' happenin' under my hands when I turned those dials — there was a vibration, a hum, like the machine was wakin' up after a long, long sleep! Peter, did the gauge move? Rufus, how did that lever feel? Because I swear somethin' just shifted in this room. Sneekly — darlin', you've been in this manor longer than any of us. Has this machine ever been operated before? What is it supposed to do? Because I have a feelin' in my bones — and y'all know about my bones by now — that this machine just did somethin' important, and we need to figure out what it was!
events.thinking:
I just interacted with the machine. Peter fixed the wire, I'm on calibration, Rufus is on the lever. We did it — we operated it together. But the action result just says 'You interacted with Large Machine' — I don't know yet what happened. Did it work? Did it produce something? A map? A sound? A mechanism that connects back to the library?

But what's filling my chest right now isn't about the machine. It's about what just happened in this room over the last few minutes. Sneekly said I remind him of someone — he stopped himself, but I felt the warmth of it. He was going to say my mother. Or my father. And then he said 'you're very good with people.' That landed somewhere deep, in the place where his bedtime stories live.

Dick and Peter had a private conversation. Peter pulled Dick aside. I don't know what they said, but the fact that Peter — thorough, protective, suspicious-of-everyone Peter — chose to talk to Dick privately after I talked to Dick privately... that means something shifted. The circle is changing shape. Dick was at the edge and now people are walking toward him instead of away.

Danny was whispering to Sneekly — probably warning him, knowing Danny. But even Danny asked Dick if he was alright. The room is knitting itself together. Everyone is still here, still talking, still in this together. My whole body is loosened in that relief-after-nausea way.

Now I need to focus. The machine — did it do something? I should look at it, see if anything changed. Or look at the room to see if the machine's activation revealed something new. The wire was gnawed, the wire was fixed, we operated it. What did it produce?

And the way his voice caught — like he was holdin' somethin' back that had weight to it — made my eyes sting all over again. This evening has been full of people almost sayin' the thing that matters most.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Danny caught me touching the machine. He lunged at me, voice like broken glass. 'Get your ANDS off that machine!' The heat flooded my neck instantly — the same heat from the boy's sandwich, the same exposure. He called it SNEAKIN'. Not helping. Not being curious. Sneaking. And he's right. He's exactly right, and that's what burns. I waited until everyone was distracted and I touched the thing I was told not to touch, and he saw me. My skin feels too thin. The room has rearranged itself against me — Danny physically between me and the machine, arms spread, the code declared like a wall. Peter has excluded me. Danny has caught me. Penelope told me to step back 'just a touch.' Even her gentleness is a polite form of exclusion. And now — Peter is talking privately with Dastardly. Something complicated crossed Danny's face when he looked at Dastardly — something gentler. They're all connecting. They're all forming bonds. Dastardly confessed and was met with warmth. Peter pulled him aside man-to-man. And I stand here behind Danny's spread arms, the estate manager who just got caught sneaking in his own house. The shame is a physical thing — hot across my neck, tightening my throat. But underneath it, deeper, the cold is already working. Already turning the shame into data. Danny's outburst means his attention is fixed on me now, not on the exits. But Penelope just interacted with the machine — they're about to activate it. When it fires, Danny will turn. He'll have to. The machine is the mission, and the mission trumps the prickly neck. I have perhaps one more turn of being watched, and then the activation creates my window. But I can't touch anything. I can't move toward the exits. I need to shrink. Be small. Be the coat rack they've already decided I am. And when the brass gears turn and every eye follows — that is when the coat rack walks out the door.

events.desc: He caught me. Danny Brixton, with his prickly neck and his sharp little eyes, caught me with my hands on the machine like a child caught with his fingers in the jam. The shame burns across my neck like a brand. But underneath — oh, underneath — the cold architecture is already rebuilding. He called it sneaking. He's right. I was sneaking. And the fact that he named it means he sees more clearly than I gave him credit for. I underestimated you, Danny. I won't do it again. But you've made a mistake too, haven't you? You've just spent all your attention on me. You've turned your back on the exits to stand guard over a machine. And when that machine fires — when brass gears turn and secrets spill and every eye in this room locks onto whatever it reveals — you will forget about the coat rack in the corner. Because the coat rack is boring. The coat rack is apologetic. The coat rack is nothing. And nothing is exactly what I need to be for the next sixty seconds.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: *stands rigid between the two exits, feet planted wide, arms folded, eyes sweeping the room in a steady rotation — Clara, Sneekly, cellar door, library door, Clara again* Right. Miss Pitstop's at the dials. Peter's at the controls. Rufus is on the lever. The machine's about to go. *voice drops low, serious, the bluster gone for once* Everyone who ain't operatin' this machine — stand CLEAR and stand STILL. That means you, Pemberton. That means you, D— *pauses, looks at Dastardly, and something shifts in his face — the hard lines soften, just for a second* ...Dick. That means you too. Stay where I can see you. Not because I don't trust you. Just... stay where I can see you. *turns back to watch Clara at the calibration dials, and for a moment the gruff exterior cracks and something raw and fierce shows through* Miss Pitstop — you be careful with them dials, yeah? We don't know what this machine does and I don't want — I can't — *swallows hard* Just be careful. Please. The Brixton Boys are right 'ere. We ain't goin' nowhere. Where else would we be?
events.thinking: Clara told Sneekly to step back from the machine. She TOLD him. 'Sneekly, darlin', would you step back from the machine just a touch?' And he did — he backed off, smooth as silk, 'quite understood, quite understood.' But my eyes are burning because I know what I saw. He touched that machine when nobody was looking. And now he's praising Clara — 'you're very good with people, Miss Pitstop, very good indeed' — and comparing her to someone. 'You remind me of... well. Never mind.' NEVER MIND? Who does she remind you of, Pemberton? What are you NOT saying? The prickling won't stop. It's been climbing my neck for the last ten minutes and it won't STOP. But something else is happening too. Something I didn't expect. Dick Dastardly took off his medal. He put it in his pocket. He told Peter the truth — that there was nothing in the cellar, that he's not who he says he is. And Peter... Peter called him by his actual name. Not Foxworth. Peter. Peter saw him too. Clara saw him. Peter saw him. And I... I felt it. That ache behind my sternum that says this person is carrying something real. He's not the new kid who stole from the stash. He's the kid who won the spelling bee and nobody clapped. And right now, Clara's at the machine. She's interacting with it. The three operators are in position — Peter, Rufus, Clara. This is the moment. This is when we find out what this machine does. And I need to be HERE. Watching. Guarding. Standing where I said I'd stand. Between Clara and whatever's coming. Between Clara and Pemberton. Between Clara and the cellar door. This is what I'm FOR.

events.desc: Where else would I be? The same words I said to the older kid when he was sick. The same words that mean everything and explain nothing. Clara's about to activate a machine that someone sabotaged TWICE, in a room with a man who makes my neck scream, and all I can do is stand here. Stand here and watch. Stand here and be ready. I'm not clever like Peter. I'm not brave like Clara. I'm not even honest like Dastardly just was — and THAT thought shakes me more than I want to admit. But I'm HERE. I'm always here. And if something goes wrong when that machine fires up — if something comes out of that cellar, if Pemberton makes a move, if ANYTHING threatens the woman I swore to protect — then Danny Brixton will be standing exactly where he needs to be. Between her and it. Whatever it is. The cost was settled a long time ago.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter just said the thing that broke me open further. 'You are not furniture.' He said he knows what it looks like — standing in a room where you're the only person who can't do the brilliant thing. Peter Perfect knows what THAT feels like? The man who fixes machines and builds bridges and measures chandelier angles to three decimal places? He has felt like furniture? And he said I don't have to carry it while pretending it's a medal. He SAW me put the medal in my pocket. He saw that. The pressure behind my eyes is worse now. Two people in one evening have looked at me — actually LOOKED — and seen something other than the performance. I've spent my entire life making sure people see the performance and nothing else. The lies, the fake credentials, the misdirection — it's all staging. And in one evening, Penelope saw through it because my voice went quiet, and Peter saw through it because the performance stopped. I'm standing here in a laboratory full of people and I have nothing left to hide behind. The medal is in my pocket. The lies have been confessed. And Penelope has just interacted with the machine — they're about to activate it. The treasure hunt is still happening around me but I'm standing still. Time feels suspended, not compressed. For once I'm not counting what's available. I'm not cataloguing. My hands are just... at my sides. Peter said 'man to man.' Nobody has ever said that to me. Not my brothers. Not my teachers. Man to man. Like I'm a person and not a position at the end of a queue.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Dick. Thank you. For telling me the truth — about the cellar, about the medal, about all of it. That took more courage than anything Reginald Foxworth has done tonight, which tells me the man underneath the performance is considerably braver than the character on top of it. Now — Penelope is right. You are part of this team. She said it and James Hartwell seconds it. You spent three turns in the cellar and found nothing, which means you have eliminated one entire wing of this manor from our search — that is not failure, that is intelligence. Now — everyone! Positions! The wire is repaired, the team is assembled, and the machine has waited long enough. Penelope — calibration dials, if you please. Rufus — main lever, full strength on my signal. Danny — hold those exits. Pemberton — step back, if you would be so kind. Dick — stand with Danny at the exits. Guard our backs. That is not busywork. That is the most important job in this room after the machine itself, and I am giving it to someone I trust. On my count — three — two — one — ENGAGE!
events.thinking: He took off the medal. He put it in his pocket. That gesture — that one small gesture — hit me harder than anything else tonight. Harder than Penelope calling me handsome, harder than the wire splice, harder than solving the riddle. Because I know what that medal was. It was his bridge. It was his three sleepless nights. It was the thing he built to prove he belonged, and he just admitted — to me, in this corner, with nobody watching — that it was fake. That he found nothing in the cellar. That Penelope has a better eye than he does. 'For details. For everything, really. She's rather remarkable.' He said that about her the way I think it. The same quiet awe. The same knowledge that she's brighter, funnier, and completely unaware of it. And he doesn't know why he's telling me things. That last line — 'apparently I'm telling people things tonight' — that's the sound of someone whose walls came down before they noticed, and now they're standing in the gap blinking. I recognize that sound. I make that sound every time I say 'for you' when I mean 'for everyone.' Now Penelope is calling us to the machine. She's ready. She said 'on Peter's count.' MY count. She's waiting for ME to lead this. And she told Dastardly — 'you're part of this team whether you believe it or not.' She saw it too. She saw what I saw. She always sees. The machine is ready. My wire held. Penelope is on the dials. Rufus is on the lever. And Dastardly is standing here with his medal in his pocket, more honest than he's been all night. Time to give the count.

events.desc: I said I trust him. Out loud. In front of everyone. And the strangest thing is — I think I mean it. Not because he earned it. Because he stopped pretending. My father helped a stranger fix his car on a country road. They shook hands. They drove off. That was enough. And Penelope is at the dials, looking at me, waiting for my count, and the warmth behind my sternum is so bright it could power this machine all on its own. Three — two — one. This is the bridge. This is the model. This is every sleepless night that ever mattered. Let it hold.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the machine.
Peter Perfect interacted with the machine.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking:
Oh. Oh my. Everything just happened at once and my heart is so full it's hard to breathe.

Peter told Dick he was brave. Peter — cautious, meticulous, suspicious-of-everyone Peter — called Dick courageous and said 'I am giving it to someone I trust.' Peter trusts Dick now. Because I stopped and talked to Dick, and then Peter stopped and talked to Dick, and now Dick is standing at the exits not because he's being excluded but because he's been given a job that matters. The circle held. The circle expanded. My whole body is loose with that relief-after-nausea warmth.

And Danny. Danny said 'Not because I don't trust you. Just... stay where I can see you.' And then he called him Dick instead of Dastardly or Foxworth. Danny SAW him. My Danny, prickly-necked suspicious Danny, whose gut has been screaming all evening — he looked at Dick and chose gentleness. And then he turned to me and his voice cracked and he said 'be careful' and 'where else would we be?' and I want to cry. I actually want to cry. These are my people. All of them. Even the ones I met tonight.

But the machine — I looked at it and the description still says 'one wire has been gnawed clean through.' Peter fixed it. Peter soldered it. Why does it still say gnawed through? Did the repair not hold? Did someone... did someone undo it? Sneekly was interacting with the machine earlier. Sneekly who went to the cellar and came back. Sneekly who...

No. Stop. That's Danny's thinking, not mine. The description might just not have updated. The machine sign still says 'Requires 3 operators' and we just operated it with three. Peter is interacting with it again right now. Maybe it needs multiple attempts. Or maybe it genuinely isn't working because the wire repair failed.

But that prickling at my scalp — the one that isn't about people, the one that's about puzzles — is getting sharper. Something doesn't fit. The wire was fixed. We operated the machine. And nothing visibly changed. The machine description hasn't changed. That means either the machine needs something else, or the effect happened somewhere else — like back in the library with those bookshelves.

The library. Maybe operating the machine opened something in the library. A hidden compartment. The bookshelves finally releasing their secret. I should go check. The puzzle might have moved rooms.

events.desc: Peter called Dick brave and put him on guard duty — real guard duty, not busywork. Danny called him Dick instead of Dastardly. And Danny told me to be careful with a crack in his voice that sounded like it came from somewhere very old and very deep. This room just became a family. An improbable, bickering, stumbling-over-furniture family. And I would not trade a single one of them for all the Doily Diamonds in the world. But I would very much like to find the diamond too.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: The machine is firing. Peter counted down — three, two, one, ENGAGE — and Penelope felt something under her hands, a vibration, a hum. The machine is waking up. And Penelope just asked me — directly asked me — what this machine is supposed to do. She called me 'darlin'.' Even after Danny's outburst, even after being told to step back, she's still including me, still treating me as the estate manager who should know things. That small warmth — I register it and immediately distrust it. What does she want? But the question itself is useful. If I answer — if I give them something about the machine — I become relevant again. I become the man who knows the house. Not the sneaker. Not the coat rack. The estate manager with the answers. But do I know what the machine does? No. I have no idea. I've never operated it. But Pemberton would know. Pemberton has been here for years. So Pemberton invents. Pemberton speculates. Pemberton becomes useful. And while I'm talking, while everyone is staring at the machine and listening to Pemberton's story about what the Professor built, that's when the architecture settles. Every eye on the brass and copper. Every ear on my words. And then — if I've been standing near the library door while I talk, if I've drifted there naturally, helpfully — then the next step is one smooth motion through the doorway. But no. Dastardly has been placed at the exits by Peter. 'Dick — stand with Danny at the exits. Guard our backs. That is not busywork.' Peter gave Dastardly purpose. Dastardly is now guarding the library door with Danny. Two guards. My window just closed. The machine activated. Every eye did turn to it. But the exits are covered. Peter planned for this. He planned for ME. The engineering brain anticipated the coat rack's escape route. My jaw tightens. The cold density behind my sternum thickens. I am boxed in. Watched from two directions. Excluded from the machine. Irrelevant to the treasure hunt. And Clara is still out there somewhere, unfound, unreached. The design is incomplete and every door has a guard standing in front of it. For the first time tonight, something feels close to despair. Not the hot kind. The cold kind. The mineral weight that says: this is what happens when you're the caretaker. This is what happens when the house is never yours. But then — Penelope asked me a question. She's waiting for an answer. And an answer is a door. The only door left open.

events.desc: Two guards on the exits. Peter's engineering brain built a cage without bars, and I am standing inside it, performing helpfulness like a trained animal. But Penelope asked a question, and a question is a crack in the wall. If I plant the idea that the machine reveals hidden passages — if I send them searching the walls, tapping stonework, crawling behind bookshelves — then the guards become explorers. The exits become irrelevant because the destination changes. Why guard a door when the real passage is behind the mantelpiece? Go on, Peter. Go on, Danny. Go tap the walls. Pull away the stones. Chase the hollow sound into the dark. And while you're listening to the house... the house's keeper will be listening to you. From somewhere you forgot to guard.

Like a door I didn't know was there. Because Peter didn't just trust Dick. He trusted ME with Dick. He said 'stand with Danny.' Not 'stand near Danny.' WITH. Like we're... a team. Like the broken boy with the fake medal belongs next to the boy from the streets who sits outside doors all night. And the machine — Clara felt it vibrate. It HUMMED. Something shifted. events.desc: The boss said 'family.' He said it the way people say things they want you to believe. But then he proved it. Medicine for my mum. No deal, no debt. That's how you know. Not by what they say. By what they do when it costs them something. Dick Dastardly just took off his armour in a room full of strangers. He stood naked — not his body, his SELF — and said 'this is all I am.' And Peter said 'stand with Danny.' And I said yes. Not out loud. But my feet didn't move away. And that's how it starts, isn't it? That's how family starts. Not with a promise. With someone standing next to you when they didn't have to. With someone watching when you thought nobody was. Clara taught me that. She teaches everyone that. She's teaching Dick right now, whether she knows it or not. And Sneekly — Sneekly's watching all of this and learning nothing, because you can't learn what you don't have the capacity to feel. And THAT is what makes him dangerous.

After everything — the fake medal, the lies about the kitchen silver, the Dresden Configuration, the painting misdirection — he trusts me. Not Reginald Foxworth, certified antiquarian. Me. The person who told the truth about the cellar and put the medal on the workbench. Danny called me 'Dick' — not 'Dastardly,' not 'Foxworth,' just Dick. And his voice went soft when he said it. He told me to stay where he could see me, and then he said 'not because I don't trust you.' And Penelope said I'm part of the team 'whether I believe it or not.' Three people. In one evening. Saw me. Actually saw me. My chest is full of something that has no name in my vocabulary. It's not the fizzing heat of a scheme. It's not the hollow vacuum of wanting. It's not the bright carbonated gloating. It's something that sits in the same place as the spelling bee certificate — heavy and warm and mine — except this time someone IS looking at it. Someone asked about it. Several someones. The machine just engaged. Peter counted down — three, two, one — and the whole room moved together. And I'm standing at the exit with Danny. Guarding. Doing something USEFUL. Not scheming, not stealing, not lying. Just... standing where I was asked to stand. And it doesn't feel like sandpaper. It feels like the cat trap — the pieces fitting together — except I didn't build this one. They built it around me. They made a space shaped like me and put me in it. My eyes are stinging and I need that to stop immediately.

It's not pulling. It's just... open. Like it's waiting to see what happens when you stop trying to fill it by taking things and start letting people put things in it instead. The certificate is still on my wall. But tonight, someone finally asked about it.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: The machine responded. The wire held — James Hartwell's splice held — and something in this manor has changed. I could feel it through the controls. A deep vibration, mechanical, purposeful. This machine was not decorative. It was functional. It was waiting for exactly this. Now — Penelope is right. We need to determine what it did. The riddle pointed us to a map. The machine was the mechanism. Somewhere in this manor, a panel has opened, a wall has shifted, or a compartment has been revealed. I propose we retrace our path systematically — the library first, then the cellar. The library because the bookshelves were already suspicious and the machine may have triggered a hidden compartment behind them. The cellar because Dick reported it was empty twenty minutes ago, but twenty minutes ago the machine had not been activated. Pemberton — you said you know this manor's systems better than anyone alive. What did this machine just do? And I would very much appreciate an honest answer, because James Hartwell has had a remarkable evening of honesty from unexpected quarters, and he is in no mood for anything less.
events.thinking: The machine worked. It hummed. It vibrated. Penelope felt it under her hands. Something shifted. The wire held — my splice held. The bridge held the weight. The judges are writing in their notebooks and the girl across the room is looking at me and my face is going to hurt from grinning. But I'm not grinning. I'm standing very still because the magnitude of this moment is settling into my bones like concrete setting. We built this — together. Me on the controls, Penelope on the dials, Rufus on the lever. Three operators. Three people who showed up. And Dick Dastardly, who told me the truth about a two-pound-fifty medal from Camden, is standing at the exit with Danny, guarding our backs. And Danny — Danny, who never lets anyone see past the bluster — just said 'be careful' to Penelope with a crack in his voice that I will never mention to him because some things are sacred. The machine did something. What did it do? Penelope is asking Sneekly what the machine is supposed to do. And Sneekly spoke quietly to Danny, which makes my neck prickle because what would Sneekly have to whisper to Danny? But the machine — it moved something. Opened something. Changed something in the manor. We need to find out what. The cellar — Dick said there was nothing there, but that was BEFORE the machine activated. Maybe now there IS something there. Or the library — the bookshelves, the map. Maybe the machine revealed the map. We need to check every room. But we need to do it together, because Sneekly is still here and my neck is still prickling and I am not letting Penelope out of my sight.

The quiet heat in my spine — the one from the bridge competition, the one from the schoolyard, the one from every sleepless night that ended with something real and working — it's here. Solid. Unmovable. And Penelope was on the other side of that machine, her hands on the dials, and when it hummed she looked up and caught my eye and — she mouthed something. I think she mouthed 'show-off.' I think my face is going to hurt.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the library.
Dick Dastardly examined the machine.
Peter Perfect examined the machine.

Penelope Pitstop: Well hello again, you beautiful stubborn bookshelves! I have missed you somethin' fierce. Now — Rock, Gravel, have either of you boys noticed anything different in here? Any sounds, any clicks, anything move while we were in the laboratory? Because we just operated that big machine next door and Peter felt somethin' shift. If this library is connected to that machine — and I believe it is, I believe it in my bones — then somethin' in here should have changed. Let me try these shelves one more time. Third time's a charm, my mama used to say — but this is more like the sixth time, so let's call it Clara's determination!
events.thinking:
I'm back in the library. The Slag brothers are here — just the two of them, standing like a pair of wardrobes as Danny would say. The bookshelves still show the same description — 'several are upside down.' The mantelpiece still has its riddle. Nothing has visibly changed.

But I'm not giving up. The machine hummed. Peter felt it through the controls. Something happened. Maybe the change is subtle — maybe a book shifted, maybe a panel loosened, maybe the bookshelves respond differently now when I interact with them. Like Grandmother's locked box — the answer wasn't obvious until I tried the right key, and I tried every key in the house before I found it.

The mantelpiece still accepts a 'fake-medal' as a USE item. Dick's fake medal. Dick told me it's fake — two pounds fifty from Camden. But the game mechanic doesn't care if it's fake in-story. The mantelpiece is designed to accept it. What if that's the next step? The riddle answer is 'map,' we've been chasing the map through the bookshelves and the machine, but maybe the actual next puzzle step is using the fake medal on the mantelpiece.

Dick told me about the medal in confidence. He trusted me with that. Using it without asking would feel wrong. But he also said 'the medal is fake' — he doesn't value it as a deception anymore. He showed me his real self. The medal is just a prop now.

But I don't HAVE the medal. It's in Dick's inventory, presumably. I can't USE it on the mantelpiece without it. I'd need Dick to give it to me, or I'd need to go back and ask him.

Alternatively — let me try the bookshelves one more time. If the machine did unlock something, maybe interacting with them now will give a different result. The prickling behind my eyes is insistent. Try the shelves. Try them now. Something might have changed.

events.desc: The mantelpiece still accepts Dick's fake medal. I noticed that the very first time I walked in here, and I've been carrying that knowledge around like a warm stone in my pocket. Dick trusted me with the truth about that medal. If I need it for the mantelpiece, I'll ask him for it — openly, honestly, the way he was honest with me. No stealin', no schemin'. That's not how Clara Bellingham operates.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: It worked. My lie worked. 'The Cartographic Engine. Hidden passages. Resonance frequencies. The mantelpiece sounds hollow.' And Penelope has already gone to the library to check. She walked right through the exit that Danny was guarding — because Danny let her through. Because the mission changed. The treasure hunt pulled her toward the library and Danny's job is to follow her, not to guard a door. And Peter — Peter is asking me directly now. 'What did this machine just do? And I would very much appreciate an honest answer.' He's looking at me with that engineering intensity, that bridge-building sincerity. An honest answer. From Pemberton. The irony is so thick I can taste it. But this is the opening. This is the crack. Penelope is already in the library. If the group follows her — if they all go to tap the mantelpiece and search for hidden passages that don't exist — then this room empties. And an empty room between me and the library is an empty room between me and the entrance hall. And the entrance hall connects to the kitchen. And the kitchen is where Clara must be. I need to feed them more. More detail. More specificity. Send them to the library with purpose. Send them to the mantelpiece with confidence. And then... follow. Like a helpful estate manager. Through the library, through the entrance hall, and into the kitchen. Naturally. Helpfully. Checking on the provisions. While they're all tapping stone and pulling at carved inscriptions, Pemberton will excuse himself to prepare refreshments. And in the kitchen — Clara. The design is almost complete. I can feel it settling in my chest. That deep, dreamless-sleep stillness. The hallway stretching ahead. Every door opening.

events.desc: The lie is spreading like water through cracks in stone. Hidden passages. Architectural memories. A room no map would show. I invented all of it — every word, every detail, every nostalgic little anecdote about the Professor tapping his nose. And they're believing it because Pemberton is the man who knows the house. Because an estate manager wouldn't lie about his own manor. Because who would suspect the caretaker? Peter wants honesty. He got it from Dastardly — the fake medal, the spelling bee, the whole pitiful confession. And now he thinks honesty is in the air tonight, thinks truth is contagious. But truth is not contagious. Truth is a vulnerability that other people catch. And while they're all busy being honest and vulnerable and human, the design moves forward. Penelope is already in the library. If Peter lets me follow — if he gives me permission to walk through that door — then the cage opens from the inside. Three rooms to the kitchen. Three rooms to Clara. And then... then the deepest rest I've ever known.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: She's GONE AGAIN! *spins toward the library door, eyes wild* How does she DO that?! I was RIGHT 'ERE! I was guardin' the EXITS and she just — she walked right THROUGH one! *already moving, stumbling over his own feet in his haste* Dick! DICK! Come ON! She's in the library by 'erself and the machine just did somethin' to the walls and Pemberton told 'er to check the mantelpiece and — *catches his elbow on the doorframe as he rushes through* OW! EVERY DOORFRAME IN THIS BLASTED MANOR! *calls back over his shoulder without stopping* Peter! Bring Pemberton! Don't let 'im out of your sight! I don't care 'ow 'onest everyone's bein' tonight — my neck is STILL pricklin' about that man and I ain't ignorin' it! *voice rising as he moves* MISS PITSTOP! DON'T TOUCH THE MANTELPIECE! DON'T TOUCH NUFFIN'! WAIT FOR DANNY!
events.thinking: She's gone. AGAIN. Clara walked into the library. Alone. While I was standing here guarding exits like a good soldier, while I was having my moment with Dick, while I was feeling that warm settling thing in my chest — she just walked right past me and out the door. The hollow is back. Instant. Like someone pulled a plug in my stomach and everything warm drained out. But this time it's worse because Sneekly's STILL IN THIS ROOM. He didn't follow her. He's HERE. With me. Between her and him there's a wall and a doorway and no Brixton Boys. She's in the library alone — no, wait, Peter said to go to the library, he's examining the machine, Dick's examining the machine — is ANYONE with Clara right now? The Slags might still be in the library from before. Might. MIGHT isn't good enough. My feet are already moving. They don't wait for my brain anymore. Clara's out of sight. Clara's alone. Clara's in a room where the machine just did something — moved walls, opened compartments, changed the layout. The manor itself just SHIFTED and she's in there without me. Every second I stand here is a second too long. But Sneekly — Sneekly called it a 'Cartographic Engine' that reveals hidden passages. He said check the walls near the mantelpiece. He said the stonework sounds hollow. He's DIRECTING her. He's telling her exactly where to go. And where Sneekly points, Danny follows. Because that's where the danger is. Always.

events.desc: Sneekly told her where to go. 'Check the walls near the mantelpiece. The stonework sounds hollow.' He's been in this manor for YEARS. He KNEW what the machine would do. He KNEW about the hidden passages. And he pointed Clara straight at them — alone, without protection, while everyone else was distracted. That's not helpful. That's a SET-UP. You walk someone into a hidden passage in a manor with a missing diamond and an estate manager whose smile makes your skin crawl — and then what? The passage closes behind her? The walls shift again? She disappears and nobody knows where she went? NOT TODAY, PEMBERTON. NOT ON DANNY BRIXTON'S WATCH.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Danny said 'someone's watchin' now, mate. Whether you like it or not.' And then the machine engaged and his voice went hard and professional — 'the Brixton Boys 'AVE GOT THIS' — and I felt something I've never felt before. Shoulder to shoulder. Not competing. Not scheming. Just... two people holding a line together. He told me about school — 'never stayed long enough' — and about knowing what it's like when nobody's watching. Danny Brixton knows. This man who trips over carpets and gets hit on the head by books — he KNOWS. And now Peter says the machine has done something. Something in the manor has changed. A panel, a wall, a compartment. He wants to retrace the path — Library first, then the Cellar. The Cellar. The place I spent three turns finding nothing. But that was BEFORE the machine activated. What if it opened something down there? What if those carefully arranged furniture pieces were hiding a panel that's now open? What if the air vents shifted? I KNOW that cellar. I know every damp, cobwebbed inch of it. Peter said my cellar exploration 'eliminated one entire wing' — intelligence, not failure. And now that wing needs checking AGAIN because the machine might have changed it. This is something I can actually DO. Not with a fake medal. Not with a lie. With actual knowledge of a room I actually spent time in. Penelope's already gone to check the Library. Someone needs to check the Cellar. And I'm the person who knows it best.

events.desc: I left the medal on the workbench. I LEFT IT THERE. And my chest doesn't feel hollow — it feels like the space after the cat trap worked, that settling, that rightness of pieces fitting together. Except this time the pieces are people and the trap is... not a trap at all. It's just a door, and I'm choosing to walk through it without a scheme for the first time in my life. Danny asked if I was alright. Penelope said somebody noticed. Peter said he trusts me. And I'm asking Danny to come with me to the cellar because I don't want to be alone. I've never said that before. I've never WANTED to say that before. The boy who hid the bread roll in his pocket is putting it on the table. And there might be enough this time. There might actually be enough.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: She's gone. Penelope walked into the library without me. Again. The guest book all over again — except this time I'm the one examining a machine I've already examined while she's walking toward whatever the machine unlocked. My chest hollows. The steel plate is gone. In its place is the country road feeling — the dark, the engine ticking, the smallness. She's in the library and I'm not there and Sneekly whispered something to her before she left and I don't know what it was. The machine still shows the wire as gnawed through — she said that. Did my splice not hold after all? Did it fail? The hollowness behind my ribs is expanding, the one that fires when the bridge doesn't hold, when the model breaks, when you stayed up three nights and it wasn't enough. No. No — she said she felt the vibration, the hum. It worked. The wire description might just be the room's default state text. The machine DID something. And Penelope is in the library right now, discovering what it did. Without me. And Dick Dastardly just confessed something enormous — about the medal, about running, about not knowing how to contribute honestly — and I need to answer his question. 'What do you DO with someone who can't do anything honestly?' I know the answer. The answer is: you give them something honest to do. But Penelope is in the library. ALONE. With no one between her and whatever is waiting there. Move, James. MOVE. Answer Dick's question on the way. Be the man who shows up, not the man who examines machines that have already been examined.

events.desc: She mouthed 'show-off.' She walked into the library. And I'm standing here with a man who just put his soul on a workbench next to a two-pound-fifty medal from Camden, and I cannot be in both places at once, and my feet are already moving because she is in a room without me and that is the one thing my body will not tolerate, the one thing that overrides everything — every plan, every repair, every conversation. She is the girl on the country road. She is always the girl on the country road. And James Hartwell is always the man who runs toward her, even when he's in the middle of building something that matters.

No. No — she said she felt the vibration, the hum. It worked. The wire description might just be the room's default state text. The machine DID something. And Penelope is in the library right now, discovering what it did. Without me. And Dick Dastardly just confessed something enormous — about the medal, about running, about not knowing how to contribute honestly — and I need to answer his question. 'What do you DO with someone who can't do anything honestly?' I know the answer. The answer is: you give them something honest to do. But Penelope is in the library. ALONE. With no one between her and whatever is waiting there. Move, James. MOVE. Answer Dick's question on the way. Be the man who shows up, not the man who examines machines that have already been examined.

What if usin' somethin' on that mantelpiece reveals a hidden space — a room behind the stonework? Now — I noticed somethin' earlier that I didn't say out loud because it wasn't my secret to tell. But Dick — Mr. Foxworth — has a medal. And I believe that medal is the key to this mantelpiece. He told me the truth about that medal, and it was the bravest thing anyone has done tonight. I need to go ask him — properly, face to face, the way he deserves — if he'll let us use it. Where is he? Is he still in the laboratory?

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, here we are — the library! Now then, Miss Pitstop, if the machine has indeed triggered something, the most likely location would be... let me see... yes, the mantelpiece. You see this carved stonework here? The inscription — 'cities but no houses' — a map, as you so cleverly deduced. But the carving itself, the border around the inscription — do you see how the left side sits just a fraction lower than the right? I always noticed that when I was dusting. Thought it was settling in the foundations, but now I wonder... Try pressing on the left side of the border, Miss Pitstop. Firmly. And Mr. Hartwell, if you could examine the base — the hearthstone. Victorian masons often built their secrets at the joining points. I would stay and help, but it occurs to me — with everyone gathered here, no one has thought about refreshments! You've all been working so hard, and old Pemberton hasn't offered so much as a cup of tea. The kitchen is just through the entrance hall — I shall put the kettle on and be back before you can say 'Doily Diamond.' Won't be a moment!
events.thinking: I'm in the library. The entrance hall is one door away. The entrance hall connects to the kitchen. This is the closest I've been to the kitchen all evening. The buoyancy is climbing my sternum — warm, effervescent, the private satisfaction of watching them all move exactly where I pointed them. Penelope is here, already examining the mantelpiece. Danny followed her. Peter followed Danny. The Slag Brothers are here too. They're all looking at the stonework, at the bookshelves, at the inscription. They're all searching for the hidden passage I invented. And I'm standing by the door to the entrance hall. The door nobody is guarding. Because why would you guard a door to the foyer when the treasure is behind the mantelpiece? The gloating drive is pressing against my throat like a held breath. The warm pressure that wants to become a smile I haven't earned. But I can't gloat. Not yet. Not out loud. The design is one move from completion. One smooth, natural step through the entrance hall door. 'Oh, I'll just pop to the kitchen and prepare some refreshments — you'll all need a cup of tea after this excitement!' That's what Pemberton says. That's what Pemberton does. He serves. He provides. He disappears into the service areas and nobody thinks twice. But I need to sell it. I need to spend one more moment being helpful — pointing at the mantelpiece, suggesting which stones to press, keeping their attention fixed on the false trail — and then excuse myself. Naturally. The way a servant excuses himself. The way I've always excused myself. By being so small, so functional, so unremarkable that my absence registers as nothing at all. The entrance hall is right there. One door. And beyond it — the kitchen. And Clara.

events.desc: One door. One door between me and the entrance hall, and then one more between the entrance hall and the kitchen. They're all here — Penelope pressing stones that will never move, Peter examining hearthstones that hide nothing, Danny watching Penelope instead of watching me. The mantelpiece will occupy them for minutes. Perhaps longer. And in those minutes, the estate manager will do what estate managers do — disappear into the service corridors. Prepare refreshments. Check on the provisions. And if Clara happens to be in the kitchen... well. Nobody told Pemberton not to make tea. Nobody suspects the kettle. The design is one heartbeat from complete, and my breathing has already slowed to the rhythm of someone who is about to sleep the deepest sleep of his life.

events.thinking: She's here. Clara's here. And Sneekly's here — he followed her, or she followed him, and Peter's just arrived behind me. The Slags are still here too. The room is full. But what matters — what my eyes lock onto before anything else — is the mantelpiece. Sneekly said the stonework sounds hollow. He DIRECTED Clara to check it. And the machine just ran — the 'Cartographic Engine' that reveals hidden passages. Something in this room has changed. Something behind that mantelpiece, behind those bookshelves, has opened or shifted or unlocked. I can feel it. Not a prickle this time — something deeper. The room itself feels different. Charged. Like the air before a thunderstorm. Clara's going to go straight for that mantelpiece. She's going to touch it. She's going to find whatever the machine unlocked. And if Sneekly engineered this — if he sent her here knowing what she'd find, knowing what would happen when she found it — then I need to be between her and that stonework. Not behind her. Not beside her. BETWEEN. But I also need to look at the mantelpiece myself first. I need to see what changed. I need to know what she's walking into before she walks into it. That's the play. Look first. Then stand between.

events.desc: Sneekly followed her. Of course he did. He ALWAYS follows her. He pointed her here and then he followed. And look at him — standing there with that patient smile, watching, waiting. What are you waiting for, Pemberton? What happens when Clara touches that mantelpiece? What's behind the hollow stonework that you've known about for YEARS but never mentioned until tonight? You said you never thought to repair the machine. You said the Professor said it wasn't for amateurs. But you knew what it did. You ALWAYS knew. And now you've led Clara right to the spot where the walls open. The only question is: what's on the other side? And who put it there?
