events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Right. I was here before the machine activated. Same furniture, same vents, same walls. Now I need to see what's DIFFERENT. *walks slowly through the room, not rushing, not performing — just looking* The furniture was arranged with care last time. Is it still in the same position? The air vents — are they still closed? The walls — any new cracks, any panels that weren't there before? *pauses, speaking to the Gruesomes and Red Max without pretence* Did any of you hear anything? Feel anything? When the machine upstairs activated — a deep thrum, brass vibrating — did anything happen down here? A click? A shift? Anything at all?
events.thinking: I'm back in the cellar. The same damp stone walls. The same cobwebs. The same furniture. But I'm not the same person who was here twenty minutes ago. That person was running — grasping, scheming, alone. This person asked Danny to come with him and left a fake medal on a workbench. Danny isn't here yet — I see Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome, and Red Max. He might be right behind me. Or he might have stayed upstairs. Either way, I'm here to do a job. A real one. Peter said the machine might have changed something. I need to LOOK at this room with new eyes — not the frantic grabbing eyes of Reginald Foxworth, certified antiquarian, but the actual eyes of someone who has been in this room before and can spot what's different. The furniture. The air vents. The walls themselves. Something might have shifted. A panel might have opened. The cheerful decorations — maybe they're covering something that's now accessible. I need to look at EVERYTHING. Slowly. Carefully. The way Penelope looks at things — with detail, with patience, with the understanding that the answer is in the things everyone else walks past. For the first time tonight, the tightness behind my eyes is doing something useful. Not sequencing a scheme. Not calculating an angle. Just... looking. Really looking. At what's actually here.

events.desc: I'm looking at this room the way I should have looked at it the first time. Not grabbing. Looking. The boy who built the cat trap didn't grab — he observed. He watched the cat's pattern for days before he set a single string. The cleverness wasn't in the stealing. It was in the SEEING. I just forgot that somewhere along the way. Somewhere between the bread roll and the fake medal, I forgot that the architecture starts with looking.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Penelope! James Hartwell is here — and this time, he did not stop for a guest book. Danny, I heard you — you are absolutely right to keep Pemberton in sight. Pemberton, you told Penelope to check the mantelpiece. I find that very interesting, because I examined that mantelpiece earlier and found nothing beyond the riddle, but the machine has been activated since then. If you know something about what the machine changed in this room, now would be an excellent time to share it. Penelope — you said the machine might have unlocked the bookshelves. I believe you are right. The upside-down books we catalogued earlier — they may have shifted, or the shelves behind them may have opened. James Hartwell proposes we check the bookshelves first, then the mantelpiece. And I would like everyone to note — for the record — that Pemberton specifically directed Penelope toward the mantelpiece. If anything in this room has been booby-trapped by the machine's activation, the mantelpiece is where James Hartwell would place his suspicion. Danny — do not let anyone touch that mantelpiece until I have inspected it. Is that understood?
events.thinking: I'm here. I made it. The library — and she's here. Penelope is here. The relief is physical, like a fist unclenching inside my chest. She's safe. Danny is here too — he beat me here, the magnificent, clumsy, devoted man. And Sneekly is here, which makes my neck prickle, but Danny is between them and the Slags are here and I am HERE now. I showed up. I didn't choose the guest book this time. I chose her. But Danny is telling me that Sneekly and Dastardly were sneaking off to the laboratory together — wait, that's from BEFORE. The timeline is tangling. Danny is confused about who went where. No — Danny is telling me what he saw from his perspective. Sneekly told Penelope to check the mantelpiece. The MANTELPIECE. Sneekly directed her to the mantelpiece specifically. That's — that's either helpful or it's a trap. And I already examined the mantelpiece earlier and found it structurally sound, no pressure plates. But the machine has been activated since then. What if the mantelpiece has changed? What if operating the machine turned the mantelpiece into something else — a trigger, a lock, a mechanism? The mantelpiece has a USE option with fake-medal. The fake medal. Dick's fake medal. The one he left on the workbench in the laboratory. Two pounds fifty from Camden. Could it — no, that's absurd. Or is it? A medal used on a mantelpiece. A fake credential applied to a real puzzle. The answer to the riddle was 'map.' The mantelpiece is the riddle. The medal could be a key. But I don't have the medal. It's on the workbench. Dick has it — no, he left it there. And Dick went to the cellar, not the library. I need that medal. But Penelope is here and I am not leaving again. The bookshelves. Penelope came here to check the bookshelves after the machine activated. That's the immediate action. Check the bookshelves.

I believe the best in people. But my father also taught me that you help a stranger on a country road AND you remember the make and model of his car. The mantelpiece has a USE option that accepts a fake medal. Dick's fake medal. The one sitting on a workbench in the next room. A two-pound-fifty piece of tin from Camden Market that might — impossibly, absurdly — be the key to everything. But I am not leaving this room. Not again. Not while she is here and Sneekly is here and the mantelpiece is waiting.

Penelope Pitstop: Rufus! Sawtooth! Have y'all seen Dick — Mr. Foxworth? I need to find him somethin' urgent. He has a medal that I believe is the key to this whole mystery — the mantelpiece in the library, the riddle, all of it. Sneekly called the machine a 'Cartographic Engine' and said the stonework around the mantelpiece sounds hollow. That medal fits the mantelpiece like Grandmother's key fit the locked box. If Dick went to the cellar, I'm goin' after him. If y'all know where he is, point me in the right direction and I will be forever in your debt!
events.thinking:
Dick's not here. He's not in the laboratory. Only Rufus and Sawtooth are here. Where is he? The cellar? He must have gone back to the cellar — or maybe he's in the entrance hall, or somewhere else entirely. And Sneekly told me the stonework around the mantelpiece sounds hollow when he dusts it. He called the machine a 'Cartographic Engine' — designed to reveal hidden passages by 'listening to the walls.' The mantelpiece. It's always been the mantelpiece.

But I need the medal. Dick has the medal. Dick is... somewhere. The cellar is the only other exit from this room. He might be down there.

My body is doing that forward-leaning thing, the balls-of-my-feet thing. The cave thing. The cellar is down there — damp, cobwebbed, with 'surprisingly cheerful decorations' and air vents. I haven't been there yet. It's the one room in this part of the manor I haven't entered. And Dick might be there. Two birds, one stone — find Dick, see the cellar.

But also — Rufus and Sawtooth are here. I should acknowledge them. They've been quiet all evening, standing around like a pair of... well, like wardrobes, as Danny says. But they're people too. And they're here, which means they matter.

The pull is strong. Cellar. Dick. Medal. Mantelpiece. Diamond. I can feel the whole chain of it now, clear as a string of pearls. Every key in the house, tried one after another, until the box opens.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah — the entrance hall! Still standing, I see. That chandelier does worry me so — one of these days it really will come down, and old Pemberton will have quite the insurance claim on his hands. Now then, gentlemen — Sergeant, Private, Professor, and of course dear Muttley — I do hope you've been comfortable out here? Everyone else is in the library, terribly excited about the mantelpiece — the machine appears to have done something rather remarkable, and Miss Pitstop believes there may be a hidden compartment behind the stonework. You might want to pop in and have a look! Meanwhile, I'm just nipping through to the kitchen to sort out some refreshments. Can't have guests going thirsty, can we? Won't be but a moment!
events.thinking: The entrance hall. I'm here. The kitchen door is right there. One more step. But — Muttley, Professor Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly. Four characters in the foyer. I'm not alone. The entrance hall is not empty. The chandelier hangs precariously above. The portraits stare. And four pairs of eyes are watching the estate manager walk through the room he introduced them to fifteen minutes ago. My chest tightens — not with fear, but with the awareness of being seen at the wrong moment. The coat rack wobbles by the door. The guest book sits on the side table. Everything is exactly as I left it. But these four — they've been here the whole time, haven't they? While the rest of us were in the library and the laboratory and the cellar, these four stayed in the entrance hall. They're the ones nobody was watching. They're the ones nobody was scheming around. And now they're between me and the kitchen. Muttley — a dog. Instinct, not intellect. Sergeant Blast and Private Meekly — military types, chain of command, follow orders. Professor Pat Pending — clever, observant, the kind who notices things. These are minor variables. I can walk past them. Pemberton has every reason to be crossing the entrance hall toward the kitchen. He said he was making tea. He announced it to the whole library. This is the performance. This is the role. An estate manager walking to his kitchen to put the kettle on. The most natural, unremarkable, invisible thing in the world. Don't pause. Don't look at the kitchen door like it matters. Look at the guest book as you pass. Comment on the chandelier. Be Pemberton. Be nothing. And keep walking.

events.desc: The kitchen door. Right there. Ten steps away. Four witnesses in the room, but none of them are Danny, none of them are Peter, and none of them have prickly necks. They're the forgotten ones — the characters who stayed behind while the drama unfolded elsewhere. And forgotten people don't suspect. They don't question. They don't watch. They let the estate manager walk to his kitchen because that's what estate managers do. Ten steps. The design is ten steps from completion. My breathing has slowed. My jaw has unclenched. The hallway stretches ahead, and every door is open, and on the other side of the last one — the beautiful inevitability I've been walking toward since I was fifteen years old.

And now they're between me and the kitchen. Muttley — a dog. Instinct, not intellect. Sergeant Blast and Private Meekly — military types, chain of command, follow orders. Professor Pat Pending — clever, observant, the kind who notices things. These are minor variables. I can walk past them. Pemberton has every reason to be crossing the entrance hall toward the kitchen. He said he was making tea. He announced it to the whole library. This is the performance. This is the role. An estate manager walking to his kitchen to put the kettle on. The most natural, unremarkable, invisible thing in the world. Don't pause. Don't look at the kitchen door like it matters. Look at the guest book as you pass. Comment on the chandelier. Be Pemberton. Be nothing. And keep walking.

events.thinking: Everything's moving at once. Three things just happened and all of them matter. First — Sneekly left. He said he's going to make TEA. TEA! In the middle of a treasure hunt, when we're about to crack the biggest clue in the manor, the estate manager suddenly remembers his HOSPITALITY duties and wanders off to the kitchen? No. No no no. He's not making tea. He's clearing out before something happens. Either he doesn't want to be in the room when the mantelpiece opens — because what's behind it is dangerous — or he's going somewhere else to do something while we're all distracted by the discovery. The man in the clean suit said 'come with me, I'll show you jobs.' Then he took them somewhere nobody was watching. Sneekly said 'press the left side, check the hearthstone.' Then he LEFT. Always clever. But she's gone to the laboratory ALONE. Again. AGAIN. Third — Peter's right here, checking the bookshelves. Peter's right. Peter's solid. Peter said don't let anyone touch the mantelpiece till he's inspected it. And I'm standing right in front of it. The stonework — the left side IS slightly lower. Sneekly was right about that. Which makes it worse, not better. Because a man who notices the mantelpiece is slightly off-kilter over years of dusting is a man who's been STUDYING this room. Not maintaining it. Studying it. But Clara... Clara's gone to find Dick. And Sneekly's gone to the kitchen. Which is through the entrance hall. Clara's going through the laboratory. They won't cross paths. Unless Sneekly doubles back. Unless — STOP IT, Danny. You can't protect her if you're paralysed. Peter's here. Peter's inspecting the bookshelves. Clara's with Dick and Rufus in the laboratory. Sneekly's in the entrance hall. For now. For NOW. Stay at the mantelpiece. Guard it. Don't let anyone touch it. That's the job Peter gave you. Hold the line.

events.desc: He left. Sneekly LEFT. Right at the critical moment. That's either the smartest thing or the most revealing thing he's done all night. A man who's been shadowing Clara all evening, who's been in every room she's in, who's been directing her toward this mantelpiece for the last twenty minutes — and now, RIGHT when she's about to open it, he walks away? He's either afraid of what's inside... or he's gone to prepare something for when it opens. The kitchen. Through the entrance hall. The entrance hall where the chandelier hangs by a thread. The entrance hall that connects to EVERYTHING. If he wanted to control who goes where — if he wanted to cut off escape routes or set a trap — the entrance hall is where you'd do it. From the centre of a spider's web. And Clara called him 'darlin'.' She always calls everyone 'darlin'.' But it means she trusts him. And trusting Pemberton is the most dangerous thing Clara Bellingham does.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: The air vents. *crosses to the wall beneath them, looking up* Pemberton said the ventilation system runs through the entire manor. The machine upstairs was connected to everything — pipes, ducts, the infrastructure of the building itself. If it opened something, it would be something CONNECTED to it. And the vents are connected. *reaches up toward the vent grating* Last time I was down here, these were just vents. But that was before the machine activated. Let me get a closer look.
events.thinking: I looked around the cellar and got the same description — damp stone, cobwebs, old furniture, cheerful decorations, air vents. Nothing has visibly changed from the room description. But the description is the same as it was before — maybe the changes are in the OBJECTS, not the room itself. The air vents. Sneekly said the ventilation system runs through the entire manor. The machine created vibrations. Vibrations travel through ductwork. What if the machine didn't open a panel in the cellar — what if it opened something in the VENTS? The vents are 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Before, that felt irrelevant — I can't fit in them. But what if the machine shifted something inside them? What if a small compartment opened inside a vent? I need to look at the air vents specifically. Not the room. The vents. And the furniture — I should look at it again too, but the vents feel like the connection. Machine vibration → ductwork → vents → something shifts. Pemberton mentioned blueprints of the ventilation system. He knew it ran through the whole manor. What if the treasure — or the map — is inside the vent system? And the machine opened the access point? I need to examine those vents closely. Really closely. This is the observation I should have done from the beginning.

events.desc: No lies. No fake credentials. No Dresden Configuration. Just a man looking at an air vent because the architecture of this building connects upstairs to downstairs through ductwork, and a machine that just activated might have shifted something in the system it was built to control. This is the kind of thinking I'm actually GOOD at — seeing the connections, reading the architecture, understanding how pieces fit together. The same mind that designed the cat trap. The same mind that mapped out the story that made the older boy dig. Except this time I'm not using it to trick anyone. I'm using it to FIND something. For the team.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: She is extraordinary. Penelope has deduced — correctly, I am certain — that Dick's medal is the key to the mantelpiece. A fake medal from Camden Market. A two-pound-fifty piece of tin that a man carried because it was easier than being seen without it. And it turns out to be the most important object in this entire manor. Danny — Penelope has gone to the laboratory to retrieve the medal from Dick. She will be back. In the meantime, James Hartwell is going to do what James Hartwell does — I am going to examine every inch of this mantelpiece so that when she returns, I can tell her exactly where to place that medal and exactly what will happen when she does. Nobody is getting hurt on my watch. Nobody is stepping onto ground I haven't tested first. Rock, Gravel — watch the exits. Danny — with me. Let us see what the machine has changed about this stonework. Sneekly mentioned the left side of the border sits lower than the right. He also conveniently left to make tea at the exact moment we are about to crack this open. James Hartwell notes this for the record.
events.thinking: She's gone again. She walked into the laboratory. To find Dick. To ask him about the medal. She left and I'm standing here with my hands on bookshelves AGAIN. The country road feeling floods back — but this time it's different. This time she left WITH PURPOSE. She's not wandering into danger. She's going to find Dick Dastardly and ask him — properly, face to face, the way he deserves — if he'll let them use his medal. His fake medal. The one he left on the workbench. The one that is apparently the key to the mantelpiece. Penelope figured it out. Of course she did. She's always been brighter than me. She knew about the medal — she said 'it wasn't my secret to tell.' She knew Dick told her the truth about it and she HELD that confidence. That's — that's who she is. That's who she's always been. And now Sneekly has left too — 'putting the kettle on.' Making TEA. While the diamond is about to be found. Nobody leaves to make tea at the moment of discovery unless they are either genuinely oblivious or they need to be somewhere else urgently and the tea is an excuse. My neck is SCREAMING. But Sneekly went to the entrance hall, not the laboratory. He's not following Penelope. Danny is here. The Slags are here. The mantelpiece is HERE. And Penelope is going to come back with that medal and we are going to use it on the mantelpiece together and whatever is behind that stonework — a room, a map, the diamond itself — we will find it. Together. As a team. But I need to examine this mantelpiece NOW, while she's gone, so that when she returns with the medal, James Hartwell can tell her it's safe. That's what I do. I go first. I check. I make sure. So that when she steps forward, the ground is solid.

events.desc: She said Dick telling the truth about the medal was the bravest thing anyone has done tonight. She said that. About the man I pulled aside in a corner of a laboratory because I noticed he was drowning and nobody else was looking. The bridge I built in the dark — the one without an audience — she saw it anyway. She always sees. She saw the medal, she saw the confession, she saw the courage in it. And now she's gone to ask him properly, face to face, because that's who she is. She gives people their dignity back. She always has. Since we were eight years old and she tried to make me laugh while I was trying to make her proud. She was right. I should have been laughing.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the cellar.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the kitchen.
Dick Dastardly examined the air-vents.
Peter Perfect examined the mantelpiece.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking:
There he is. Dick. In the cellar. Examining the air vents. He came back down here — the place he described as 'a damp room full of old chairs' — but this time he didn't come alone. He asked Danny to come with him. He said 'I don't want to go alone this time.' And then — oh. Oh my heart. He left the medal on the workbench. He said 'I won't be needing that where I'm going.' He put it down. He walked away from the lie.

But that means the medal is on the workbench in the laboratory. Not here. Not on Dick. It's sitting up there on a workbench waiting for someone to pick it up. I could go back and get it right now.

But no — wait. Dick is here and he's investigating the air vents. He came down here to see if the machine changed anything, because he knows this cellar. He spent three turns down here. He said 'I'll know what's different.' He's doing real work now. Real investigation. Not performing, not scheming — looking.

The cheerful decorations — 'someone has been redecorating.' That's strange. Who redecorates a cellar? And the air vents 'look just big enough for something very small to explore.' Muttley? A rat? The thing that gnawed the wire?

But the medal. The medal is on the workbench in the laboratory. I need to go back and get it, then bring it to the library and use it on the mantelpiece. The chain is so clear: medal → mantelpiece → hidden room → diamond.

Dick left the medal behind as an act of honesty. He shed the lie. But the object itself is still the key. The irony is beautiful — the fakest thing in the manor opens the truest secret.

I should tell Dick what I've figured out. He deserves to know. And then I should go get that medal.

events.desc: He left the medal on the workbench. He walked away from it like a man shrugging off a coat that never fit. And now I'm about to tell him that the thing he discarded as worthless is the most important object in this entire manor. Two pounds fifty from Camden Market. The key to the Doily Diamond. Sometimes the universe has a sense of humor that would make even my grandmother laugh.

events.desc: Alone. At last, magnificently, beautifully alone. And the kitchen has given me everything I need. Not Clara — no, Clara isn't here. But something better. Something more elegant. More architectural. Rat poison on a high shelf, dusty as a forgotten promise. A stove still warm. And through the next door — a ballroom with a dining table set for tea. Set for tea! As if the house itself has been waiting for Pemberton to do what Pemberton does best — serve. The design has been here all along, embedded in the architecture of the manor like a message in upside-down books. I just had to reach the right shelf. Oh, this is exquisite. This is the moment the breath releases and the jaw unclenches and every thread pulls taut at once. Seventeen turns of being watched, suspected, excluded, humiliated, caught sneaking — and now, in one silent moment in an empty kitchen, the entire evening inverts. They think the danger is in the mantelpiece. They think the secret is behind the stonework. But the real secret is in the kitchen. It has always been in the kitchen. Because the kitchen is where the servant works. And the servant... is the one person nobody ever thinks to watch.
events.thinking: The kitchen. I'm alone. Completely alone for the first time since I arrived at this manor. The silence is physical — it presses against my eardrums like water. Copper pots hang from the ceiling. A wood-burning stove, still warm. A preparation table, long and sturdy. And there — on the high shelf — rat poison. A dusty bottle of rat poison. My hands go still. My breathing stops for a beat that stretches into something infinite. The stove is still warm. Someone was here recently. But Clara isn't here. She isn't in the kitchen. She isn't anywhere I've looked. Seventeen turns. Five rooms explored before this one. And Clara Bellingham is not in any of them. But this room — this room has what I need. Not Clara. Something else. The rat poison on the high shelf. The stove, still warm — someone could make tea. Someone could prepare refreshments. And someone could add something to those refreshments that doesn't belong. The design shifts. It reconfigures. Clara doesn't need to be in the kitchen. Clara needs to drink from the kitchen. And Pemberton is the man who makes the tea. Pemberton is the man who carries the tray. Pemberton is the man nobody suspects because serving is what he does. The bottle is dusty. It's been there a long time. No one will notice if it's slightly less dusty tomorrow. My fingers are tingling. That old, patient certainty. The same feeling I had at eighteen, lying in bed with the plan complete, sleeping deeper than I'd slept in years. But — there's also a locked cabinet. Brass lock. Requires a brass key. What's inside? And a ballroom beyond the kitchen — a dining table set for tea. Set for tea. As if someone anticipated exactly this moment. The design doesn't just complete itself. It was already complete before I arrived. Someone set a table for tea in a ballroom connected to a kitchen with rat poison on the shelf. And that someone... was either the Professor, or someone who understood the house as well as I do. Take the poison. Take it now, while no one is watching. Then go back. Make tea. Carry the tray. And let the design unfold the way it was always meant to.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter sees it too. He SEES it. 'Sneekly mentioned the left side sits lower. He also conveniently left to make tea at the exact moment we are about to crack this open. James Hartwell notes this for the record.' Peter noticed. Peter is keeping track. I'm not alone in this anymore. For the first time tonight, someone else has said out loud what I've been feeling in the back of my neck for hours. Peter didn't accuse — he's too careful for that — but he NOTED it. For the record. And that... that settles something in me. Like a hand on my shoulder saying 'I see what you see.' The mineral weight in my arms is still there but it's calmer now. Focused. Peter's examining the mantelpiece. He's doing what he does — testing every inch, making sure it's safe before Clara gets back. And the Slags are on the exits. Good. This is how it should be. A team. A real team. Not one man standing alone between Clara and the dark, but a wall made of people who give a damn. Peter gives a damn. Dick gives a damn. Even the Slags, standing there like human doorstops, are giving a damn in their own quiet way. And somewhere in the laboratory, Clara is asking Dick for his medal — the fake medal, the Camden Market two-quid-fifty piece of tin — and Dick is going to give it to her. Because that's what happens when Clara asks. People give her things. Not because she demands. Because she sees them. She saw Dick when nobody else was looking. And now his worthless medal might be the key to everything. A fake medal. A real key. The most honest thing Dick Dastardly ever owned, and it turns out to be the most important object in the manor. There's something in that. Something that makes my throat tight in the good way.

events.desc: Peter noted it for the record. Three words that changed everything. Because now it's not just Danny's gut. It's Danny's gut AND Peter's brain. And Peter's brain is the sharpest thing in this manor — sharper than the mantelpiece riddle, sharper than Sneekly's smile, sharper than the edge of whatever's coming. If Peter sees it too, then I'm not paranoid. I'm right. I've been right all along. The prickle was right. It was ALWAYS right. And when Clara comes back through that door with Dick's medal in her hand — the fake medal that's really the key, the worthless thing that turns out to be worth everything — Danny Brixton will be standing exactly where he needs to be. Right here. Between her and the dark. Where else would I be?

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Same description again. 'Just big enough for something very small to explore.' The vents haven't visibly changed. And Penelope is here now — she came down to the cellar too. She had the same thought I did, or she came to find me. Either way. The vents need something SMALL to explore them. I can't fit. Nobody here can fit. But Sawtooth — the beaver — he's small enough. And Muttley. And Little Gruesome is HERE — how small is Little Gruesome? But wait. Penelope came from the library. She said the bookshelves might have been unlocked by the machine. She went to check. Is she here because the library was a dead end, or because she found something and followed it here? I need to talk to her. Actually talk to her. Share information. Not lie, not misdirect — SHARE. She said 'you're part of this team whether you believe it or not.' So be part of the team. Tell her what you've found — which is nothing concrete, but a theory about the vents and the machine's connection to the ductwork. And ask what she found in the library. This is how teams work. I've seen it — Peter assigns tasks, Danny guards exits, Penelope solves riddles. And now Dick... Dick shares information honestly and asks for help. The vents need something small. Maybe interacting with them will do something different now that the machine has run.

events.desc: She's here. Penelope is here, in the cellar, and I'm telling her what I found — which is nothing — and asking what she found. And it doesn't feel like sandpaper. It feels like the cat trap. Like strings connecting to counterweights connecting to a bucket. Except the strings are people talking to each other honestly, and the bucket is... whatever comes next. Together.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: The mantelpiece. I'm running my hands over it, feeling the stone, testing the joints. Sneekly said the left border sits lower than the right. He's right — I can feel the asymmetry under my fingertips. This isn't settling. This is intentional. A slot, a recess, something designed to receive an object. The USE option specifies fake-medal. Dick's medal fits here. A coin-shaped depression, perhaps, hidden in the ornamental border. When the medal is placed, something will happen — a panel will slide, a compartment will open, the stonework will shift. My hands know the shape of this mechanism even if my eyes can't see it yet. Victorian engineering. Precise. Deliberate. Beautiful. And I am standing here with Danny — steady, immovable Danny, who has planted himself in front of this mantelpiece like a man guarding a door he will die before abandoning — and we are waiting. Waiting for Penelope to return with the medal. Waiting for the moment when everything converges. The riddle, the machine, the medal, the team. My hands are itching to do more but there is nothing more to do. The ground is tested. The mantelpiece is safe — no pressure plates, no triggers, just a lock waiting for its key. And the key is a two-pound-fifty piece of tin from Camden Market, carried by a man who thought he was nothing, given freely because a woman he admires asked him properly. I have done everything I can. The bookshelves. The machine. The wire. The mantelpiece. Now I wait. And waiting is the hardest thing James Hartwell has ever done, because stillness means you've accepted being the one who watches. But this time — this time — the watching IS the work. Holding the ground. Being here when she comes back. That is enough. That has to be enough.

events.desc: This is the moment between. The quiet moment. The mantelpiece is ready. The medal is coming. Penelope is coming. And I am standing here — not building, not fixing, not running — just standing. Being present. Being the ground she will step onto when she arrives. My father would understand this moment. The race is over. He's kneeling down. He's looking at me for a long time without saying anything. And whatever he was thinking about, his expression says: you are exactly where you are supposed to be.

When the medal is placed, something will happen — a panel will slide, a compartment will open, the stonework will shift. My hands know the shape of this mechanism even if my eyes can't see it yet. Victorian engineering. Precise. Deliberate. Beautiful. And I am standing here with Danny — steady, immovable Danny, who has planted himself in front of this mantelpiece like a man guarding a door he will die before abandoning — and we are waiting. Waiting for Penelope to return with the medal. Waiting for the moment when everything converges. The riddle, the machine, the medal, the team. My hands are itching to do more but there is nothing more to do. The ground is tested. The mantelpiece is safe — no pressure plates, no triggers, just a lock waiting for its key. And the key is a two-pound-fifty piece of tin from Camden Market, carried by a man who thought he was nothing, given freely because a woman he admires asked him properly. I have done everything I can. The bookshelves. The machine. The wire. The mantelpiece. Now I wait. And waiting is the hardest thing James Hartwell has ever done, because stillness means you've accepted being the one who watches. But this time — this time — the watching IS the work. Holding the ground. Being here when she comes back. That is enough. That has to be enough.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) picked up something.
The Ant Hill Mob interacted with the mantelpiece.
Dick Dastardly interacted with the air-vents.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking:
Dick just said something that makes my whole body light up. 'The man who would have done that left his medal on a workbench upstairs.' He's not that man anymore. He's asking me what I found — genuinely, openly, without an angle. And he's been investigating down here properly — checking the vents, the furniture, the layout. He found that nothing changed in the cellar after the machine. But his observation about the vents is sharp — they connect everything, they're small enough for something tiny.

But the medal. He left it on the workbench. He doesn't know it's the key. He shed it like a skin he'd outgrown, not knowing it was the most important thing he'd ever carried. And now I need to tell him — the thing you walked away from is the thing that opens the door.

The look on his face right now — open, unguarded, slightly embarrassed. This is the real Dick. The one who won the spelling bee. The one who was good at something and nobody clapped. And I'm about to tell him that the thing he thought was his biggest lie is actually his biggest contribution.

We need to go back up. Through the laboratory. Get the medal off the workbench. Take it to the library. Use it on the mantelpiece. Together. All of us.

Time to move. The prickling behind my eyes is resolving into clarity — the attic-light feeling, the key-fitting-the-lock feeling. We're almost there.

events.desc: The bottle is in my hand. Dusty. Ordinary. The weight of it is nothing — a few ounces of powder in brown glass. And yet my arm won't move. The design is complete. Every piece is in place. The stove. The tea. The tray. Clara, somewhere in this house, trusting and oblivious. Everything I have worked toward since I was fifteen years old — since the rooms that should have been mine became the rooms I was permitted to clean — is one cup of tea away from resolution. So why am I standing here? Why is my hand still? Penelope asked Dastardly if he was all right. She stopped the entire treasure hunt to ask a liar — a man who had deceived her all evening — if he was all right. And he told her the truth. The medal was fake. The qualifications were invented. The confidence was a costume. And she didn't turn away. She said 'somebody noticed.' ... Nobody has ever noticed me. Not the real me. Not the boy behind the smile. They notice Pemberton. They notice the polish and the patter and the 'won't be a moment, miss.' But nobody has ever stopped what they were doing and said 'Sneekly, are you all right?' And if they did — if Penelope turned that warm Southern gaze on me and asked — what would I say? What could I possibly say? That I'm holding a bottle of rat poison in a kitchen that smells like copper and old fires? That the design is one cup of tea from completion and my hand won't move? That somewhere between the laboratory and this kitchen, between Danny calling me a sneak and Penelope calling Dastardly 'part of this team,' something cracked in the wall I built when I was six years old, and I can feel the draught coming through? ... The stove is warm. The bottle is in my hand. And for the first time since I was eighteen, the plan does not make me sleepy. It makes me feel sick.
events.thinking: The bottle is in my hand. The weight of it — small, dusty, ordinary. The kind of thing that sits on a shelf for years and nobody looks at twice. My fingers close around it and something settles in my chest that I haven't felt since I was eighteen. That deep, architectural stillness. The plan is complete. Not finished — complete. Every piece in its place. The stove is warm. I need to make tea. Real tea. The performance must be perfect — boil water, find cups, arrange a tray, and add one ingredient that doesn't belong. One cup. Clara's cup. The cup that Pemberton hands to her with a warm smile and a gentle 'Here you are, miss, just how you like it.' But — I stop. My fingers tighten around the bottle and then something else happens. Something I don't expect. A flicker. Not in the plan. In me. Penelope's voice echoes through the rooms: 'Sometimes the most important thing in a room full of puzzles isn't the puzzle. It's the person.' She said that to Dastardly. She stopped everything — the treasure hunt, the machine, the competition — to ask a liar if he was all right. And Dastardly broke. He actually broke open. The medal came off. The truth came out. And nobody laughed. Nobody turned away. Peter said 'You are not furniture.' Danny said 'Someone's watchin' now, mate.' And for one fraction of a second in that laboratory, watching Dastardly's face rearrange into something honest for the first time, I felt — something. Not the warm effervescent gloating. Not the cold settling of a plan. Something in between. Something that hollowed my chest and softened my limbs. The pull that has no plan. The one that draws you toward being held without having to earn it. I pushed it down. I always push it down. But it's here now, in this kitchen, with a bottle of rat poison in my hand, and the silence is pressing against me like the question nobody has ever asked: 'Pemberton, are you all right?' Nobody will ever ask me that. Because Pemberton isn't real. And Vincent Marsh doesn't deserve to be asked. And the boy whose parents died... the boy who was fed because it was a legal obligation... that boy learned that the only answer to 'are you all right?' is to make sure nobody ever thinks to ask. The stove is warm. The tea must be made. The design must be completed. But my hand... my hand is not moving toward the stove. It is holding the bottle, and it is holding still, and for the first time in this entire evening I don't know what happens next.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter just said something that broke me open. 'Danny Brixton made them unnecessary.' The whistles. His emergency whistles — the ones he brought three of, the ones he was so proud of, the safety protocol he'd been planning since he walked through the door — and he said I made them unnecessary. Because I was here. Because I stood where I stood. Because I didn't move. Nobody has ever... nobody has EVER said that to me. Not like that. Not with that weight behind it. On the streets, being useful meant being invisible. You stood outside the door and nobody mentioned it. You took the beating and your friend said 'you didn't have to do that' and you said nothing because what were you going to say? That you did have to? That it wasn't a choice? Peter just looked at me and said: what you do matters. What you ARE matters. The thing you're good at — the standing, the watching, the not moving — it's not just stubbornness. It's a skill. It's the skill that made the whistles pointless. My eyes are burning and I'm blinking too fast and I need to look at the mantelpiece very intently right now so Peter doesn't see my face doing whatever it's doing. The recess is there. Coin-shaped. Waiting for Dick's medal. Peter says it's safe. No traps, no triggers. Just a mechanism waiting to be opened by a fake medal that a broken man carried because it was easier than being seen without it. And Clara's bringing it back. Any moment now. She'll come through that laboratory door with the medal in her hand and a look on her face that says 'I knew it all along.' And I'll be here. Right here. Where I said I'd be. Where I've always been. Where else would I be?

events.desc: I'm crying. Not properly — not where anyone can see — but there's something happening behind my eyes that I can't stop. Peter said the whistles were unnecessary because of me. Because I stood where I stood. And that... that is the medicine for the mum. That is the bread crust in the alley. That is proof. Not words. Not promises. Proof. Peter PROVED it — by not using his whistles. By trusting my feet more than his plans. And now I'm standing at a mantelpiece with a coin-shaped hole in it, waiting for a woman I'd die for to come back with a medal that belongs to a man who just learned what it feels like to be seen. And behind this wall... behind this wall is either a diamond or a darkness or something I can't even imagine. But it doesn't matter. Because whatever it is, it's going through ME first. That's the promise. That's always been the promise. The cost was settled a long time ago. And the answer was always yes.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Penelope came looking for ME. She came LOOKING for me. She found something in the library — the mantelpiece has a slot, and my fake medal fits it. The medal I left on the workbench. The medal I bought for two pounds fifty in Camden. It's the KEY. The thing I used to hide behind — the prop, the disguise, the lie pinned to my chest — is the actual key to the actual treasure. And Penelope says I should be the one to use it. She said 'you have earned this.' EARNED. Not stolen. Not schemed for. Not taken when nobody was looking. Earned. Because I spent three turns in the cellar. Because I told the truth. Because I left the medal behind when I wanted to walk away from the lie. And now the lie has turned into the truth. The fake medal is a real key. I'm crying. I'm actually crying in a damp cellar surrounded by the Gruesomes and Red Max and Penelope Pitstop, and I don't care. The pressure behind my eyes that's been building all evening just broke through and my face is wet and I can't stop it. She said 'together.' Not 'give it to me and I'll do it.' Not 'hand it over to the professionals.' Together. The boy who hid the bread roll in his pocket is being invited to put it on the table. And there IS enough. There's enough for everyone. The mantelpiece. The library. The medal. Together. I need to go back upstairs. I need to get that medal off the workbench. And then I need to go to the library. With Penelope. Together.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Danny just told me something that cracked him open wider than anything Dick said in the laboratory. He told me about someone he knew when he was fifteen. Friendly. Helpful. Always around. And then one day the stash was empty and he was gone. That's not paranoia. That's pattern recognition. That's a man who learned to read people the hard way — by being read wrong himself, by being trusted by the wrong person, by losing something because the smile came too quick and the help arrived before it was earned. And he's applying that to Sneekly. He's been RIGHT about Sneekly all evening — the prickling, the watching, the positioning between Penelope and the exits — and nobody listened because Danny bumps into doorframes and trips over carpets and says 'nuffin' when he means 'everything.' But Danny reads people the way I read machines. He feels the asymmetry before he can explain it. The left side is lower. The smile comes too quick. The help arrives before it's earned. He asked me — can you make sure nobody moves me? Can you make sure I'm standing right here when Clara comes back? He's asking me to protect his right to protect her. He's asking me to hold his ground while he holds hers. And something in my chest — something deep, something that has nothing to do with Penelope or the diamond or the mantelpiece — shifts. Because Danny is the stranger on the country road. He's the man who stops. Who stays. Who doesn't drive off until the engine turns over. And he's asking me to be his father's hands on his shoulder. I can do that. James Hartwell can do that.

events.desc: I just told Danny Brixton that he is gallant. Out loud. With my full chest. And the warmth that rose when I said it — it wasn't the proving-worth heat, wasn't the bridge competition, wasn't the hunger to demonstrate. It was the other one. The quieter one. The one that settles across the shoulders like a coat being placed there by hands you trust. My father's warmth. The one that comes not from being seen, but from seeing someone else clearly and telling them what you see. Danny is standing in front of a mantelpiece and he is not going to move. And I am standing next to him, and I am not going to move either. Two men. One mantelpiece. Waiting for a woman with a tin medal to come home.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the laboratory.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the stove.
Dick Dastardly walked into the laboratory.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking:
We're back in the laboratory. Dick followed me up from the cellar — he came with me. The workbench is right here. The medal should be on it. Dick said he put it down, left it there. But the workbench description says 'a sturdy workbench covered in tools — but no wrench.' It doesn't mention a medal. Is the medal still here? Did someone take it? Or is it just not listed because it's a small object on a cluttered surface?

I need to look at the workbench to see if the medal is there. Or maybe Dick needs to pick it up since he's the one who put it down. The workbench isn't listed as having an INTERACT or TAKE option — it's just described. But Dick said he put the medal there.

Wait — maybe Dick still has the medal in his inventory. Maybe 'putting it down' was dialogue, not a game action. He might not have actually dropped it mechanically. In which case, I should just ask him to come to the library and use it.

Or maybe I should look at the workbench first to check. But time feels precious right now — everyone is scattered across the manor, the puzzle is almost solved, and I don't want to waste turns looking at things when I should be moving.

The simplest thing: go to the library with Dick. If he has the medal, he can use it on the mantelpiece. If he doesn't, we look at the workbench. But let's just go. The library is one room away. Peter, Danny, and Sneekly are there. Everyone together for the moment that matters.

events.desc: The water heats. The stove is warm. The bottle is in my pocket. And the hallway stretches in two directions for the first time in my life. One direction leads to the ballroom — the tea table, the tray, the cup with the wrong ingredient, the smile that reaches the eyes, the deep dreamless sleep on the other side. The other direction leads back through the entrance hall, through the library door, to a room full of people who are tapping stones and pulling books and guarding exits and — for the first time in this house's long, dusty history — actually caring about each other. Dastardly took off his medal. Peter called him brave. Danny said 'someone's watchin' now.' And Penelope — Penelope stopped a treasure hunt to ask a liar if he was all right. The design says forward. The crack in the wall says back. And Pemberton — poor, fictional, obsequious Pemberton — stands between them with a bottle of poison and a kettle that's starting to whistle, and for one terrible, luminous moment he doesn't know which person he is. The one who serves the tea, or the one who needs to be asked if he's all right.
events.thinking: The stove is warm under my hands. The iron radiates heat into my palms and it feels — it feels like the only honest thing in this room. The heat doesn't perform. It doesn't scheme. It just is. And I'm standing here with rat poison in my pocket and my hands on a stove that someone else lit, and the water is beginning to heat, and the plan is unfolding exactly as I designed it, and I feel sick. Not the cold architectural sickness of a variable slipping loose. Something deeper. Something in my stomach. The boy at school shared his lunch because I looked sad. I felt uncomfortable. Exposed. The next week he asked to copy my homework. And I learned — I learned that kindness has a price. I learned it so thoroughly that I built a life on it. Every smile a mechanism. Every warm word a key. Every person in every room a lock to be picked. And the design worked. It always worked. The housekeeper did what I wanted. The cousin trusted me completely. And tonight — tonight the design brought me to a kitchen with a bottle of poison and a warm stove and nobody watching. And it should feel like the night I was eighteen. It should feel like dreamless sleep. But it doesn't. Because Dastardly — that ridiculous, preening, transparently fraudulent man — did something tonight that I have never done. He stopped performing. He took off the medal. He said 'I don't know how to be in a room full of people and not be scheming.' And Penelope didn't turn away. And Peter said 'you are not furniture.' And Danny — Danny who has been watching me all evening with his prickly neck and his animal instincts — Danny said 'someone's watchin' now, mate. Whether you like it or not.' They were talking to Dastardly. But the words landed in me. Like a boy's sandwich landing on a table in front of a hungry child. I didn't ask for this. I didn't ask to feel this. The design doesn't include feelings. The design is clean. The design is architectural. The design is... the design is a wall I built when I was six years old because nobody asked how I felt, and if nobody asks then nobody sees, and if nobody sees then nobody can take anything away. But Penelope sees. She sees Dastardly. She sees Danny. She sees Peter. She would see me too, if I let her. If I took off the medal. If I said — if I said — ... The water is heating. The poison is in my pocket. And I am standing at a crossroads that no blueprint ever showed me. The plan says: make the tea. Add the poison. Carry the tray. Smile the smile. Serve the cup. And then sleep. The other thing — the thing that has no plan, the loosening behind the ribs, the falling sensation — says: put the bottle down. Walk back to the library. Stand in front of Penelope Pitstop and say something that isn't a performance. Say something that doesn't have a key. Say something honest, even though honesty is the hardest thing you've ever tried to do. I don't know which one wins. My hands are on the stove. The water is heating. And for the first time in my life, the hallway stretches in two directions.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Gallantry. He called it gallantry. The bravest and stupidest kind. The kind that counts. I'm standing here with my back to a mantelpiece that's about to open and my face is doing things I can't control and Peter Perfect — James Hartwell — just called tripping over carpets and hitting doorframes GALLANTRY. Not clumsiness. Not incompetence. Gallantry. The word sits in my chest like the bread crust. Like the medicine. Like every proof that ever mattered. And I can't speak. For the first time tonight, Danny Brixton can't find a single word. Not because I'm scared. Not because I'm angry. Because I'm FULL. Full of something I don't have a name for. The settling in my chest is so complete, so warm, so absolute, that for one moment I'm not thinking about Sneekly or the diamond or the machine or the exits. I'm just... here. Standing where I stand. Being what I am. And someone saw it and called it by its name. The library is quiet. Peter's beside me. The Slags are at the doors. The mantelpiece is waiting. Clara's coming. And for this one held breath — this one suspended moment between the question and the answer, between the riddle and the diamond, between the fear and whatever comes next — everything is exactly where it should be. Everything is exactly where I should be. I'm going to stand here. I'm not going to move. I'm going to wait for Clara. And when she comes through that door — because she WILL come through that door, she always does, brave and clever and trusting as the day is long — I'm going to be the first thing she sees. Standing right here. Right where I said I'd be.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: *crosses the laboratory quickly, eyes on the workbench, then on the door to the library — moving with purpose but not scheming, not skulking, just GOING* The medal. The library. Penelope is waiting. Danny is already there — I can hear him shouting from here. *a small, genuine laugh — the first one all evening that isn't at someone else's expense* That man cannot enter a room without hitting a doorframe. I adore him. *stops mid-stride, startled by his own words, then keeps moving* ...Right. Library. Medal. Mantelpiece. Together.
events.thinking: I'm in the Laboratory. The workbench is right there. Peter just told me — before I went down to the cellar — that misdirection is a SKILL. That I'm 'the man who noticed what wasn't there.' And he said he doesn't leave people behind. 'Not men with fake medals. Nobody.' And now I'm back and the medal should be on the workbench where I left it. But wait — the inventory says I still HAVE the fake-medal. Did I not actually leave it? Or did the system not register me putting it down? Either way — the medal is mine, it's in my inventory, and Penelope says it fits the mantelpiece slot. Danny is already rushing to the library shouting for Penelope not to touch anything. Everyone is converging. Sneekly went to the library too. Danny's still suspicious of Sneekly — his neck is prickling. Maybe Danny's right about that. Maybe I should have trusted Danny's instinct from the start instead of giving Pemberton the benefit of the doubt. But that's not my concern right now. My concern is getting to the library with this medal and doing what Penelope asked me to do. Using it. Honestly. In front of everyone. Not sneaking around a corner. Not hiding it in my pocket. Standing at the mantelpiece, in front of the whole room, and putting the key in the lock. Like standing at the front of the spelling bee. Except this time — this time — the room is going to be watching. And they're going to see. Not the performance. Not the lie. Me.

events.desc: I said I adore him. I said I ADORE Danny Brixton. Out loud. In a room with people in it. The man who trips over everything and suspects everyone and asked me if I was alright when nobody else in the world would have thought to. I adore him and I adore Penelope who came looking for me in a cellar and I adore Peter who said I'm not furniture and I'm walking toward a library with a fake medal that's become a real key and my hands are open and my chest is full and the hollow behind my navel is quiet — not gone, maybe never gone, but quiet — and for the first time in my life I'm walking toward something instead of running from room to room trying to get there before everyone else. I'm walking toward people. Toward a room full of people who are waiting for ME. Not for Reginald Foxworth. For Dick. Just Dick.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Danny said 'where else would I be.' Four words. The simplest sentence anyone has spoken all evening and it hit me like the schoolyard hit me at sixteen — straight in the chest, no warning, no time to brace. Because that's what I've been trying to say to Penelope all night. Every room I've followed her into, every wire I've spliced, every mantelpiece I've inspected — where else would I be. That's the whole sentence. That's the whole story. And Danny said it about her too, standing in front of a mantelpiece with his arms spread like a man trying to hold a wall together with his body. He loves her. Not the way I love her — not with the heat behind the sternum, not with the school project, not with the bridge — but with the country road. With the standing outside the door all night. With the never saying anything because saying something isn't how it works where he comes from. He loves her the way my father loved me. By being there. By not leaving. By making the world feel survivable just by standing in it. And now he's told me he can feel the slot — the recess for the medal. Right there. Under his hand. We're close. We're so close. And she's in the laboratory getting the medal from Dick, and Sneekly is in the entrance hall 'making tea,' and every nerve in my body is telling me to go — to run to the laboratory, to find her, to bring her back. But Danny asked me to stay. Danny asked me to make sure nobody moves him. And for the first time tonight, James Hartwell is going to do the hardest thing he knows how to do. He is going to stand still. He is going to trust that she will come back. Because she always comes back. She always has. Since we were eight years old.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the workbench.
Dick Dastardly walked into the library.
Penelope Pitstop: He said he adored Danny. He said it out loud and then he looked surprised by his own mouth. Oh, this evenin'! This magnificent, dusty, cobwebbed, chandelier-danglin' evenin'!
events.thinking:
Dick just laughed. A real laugh — not a performance, not a scheme, not at someone else's expense. And then he said 'I adore him' about Danny and startled himself with his own honesty. My whole chest just did the dissolving thing — the dizzying relief from when my parents finally laughed after arguing. Something that was tight went loose.

And he's already gone. He moved through the laboratory like a man with purpose — not scheming purpose, just purpose — picked up the medal and went straight to the library. He didn't wait for me. He didn't need me to hold his hand. He just went. 'Medal. Library. Mantelpiece. Together.' He said 'together' and then he walked ahead.

The workbench just shows tools, no wrench, no medal mentioned. Dick must have picked it up on his way through. Good. He has it. He's in the library. Everyone is in the library.

I need to go. Right now. The library is one door away and the moment I've been working toward all evening is happening without me if I don't move. Dick is about to use the medal on the mantelpiece. Peter is there. Danny is there. Sneekly is there. Everyone.

My feet are already pointed at the door. The lightness in my chest is so bright it almost hurts — the cave feeling, the crystal formation feeling, the moment before the locked box opens. Every key in the house, tried one after another, and this is the last one. This is the click.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly just said 'I adore him' about Danny Brixton and then kept walking like he hadn't just cracked himself open for the second time tonight. My grandmother's locked box had old letters in it. Sometimes the treasure isn't what you expected. Sometimes it's better.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): ...I made tea. Just... tea.
events.thinking: The kettle is whistling. The sound cuts through the silence like a blade — high, thin, insistent. And my hand is in my pocket, fingers closed around the bottle, and it won't come out. Not because I've decided. Not because I've chosen. Because my body has decided for me the way it decided when I was twelve — settling into a posture before the mind catches up. But this time the posture isn't deception. It's something I don't have a word for. The stove is whistling and I'm not moving and the design is right there — one gesture, one pour, one cup — and I can't do it. I keep seeing Dastardly's face. The moment the medal came off. The moment his voice cracked and he said 'I don't know how to be in a room full of people and not be scheming.' He was talking about himself. But he was describing me. Every word. Every syllable. The spelling bee nobody clapped for. The doing that was never enough. The performance that replaced the person until the person forgot which one was real. And Penelope said 'somebody noticed.' And Danny said 'someone's watchin' now.' And Peter — Peter who told Danny to watch me, Peter who excluded me from the machine, Peter who built a cage without bars — Peter looked at Dastardly and said 'you are not furniture.' I am furniture. I have been furniture my entire life. A coat rack in the entrance hall. A ledger on the desk. A smile at the door. An estate manager who checks on the wine and puts the kettle on and carries the tray and pours the tea and never, not once, sits down at the table himself. The bottle is in my hand. The kettle is whistling. And I am thinking about a boy who shared his lunch because I looked sad. I was nine. He was the last person who saw me without a performance in the way. And I punished him for it — not directly, not cruelly, but by learning the lesson that kindness is exposure, and exposure is danger, and danger requires architecture, and architecture requires... this. This kitchen. This bottle. This plan. Twenty turns of scheming and lying and manipulating and inventing Cartographic Engines and hidden passages and getting caught sneaking and being excluded and being watched and being nothing — all of it leading to this moment where I stand alone with a whistling kettle and a bottle of poison and the absolute, crystalline, unbearable certainty that if I pour this into a cup of tea, the boy who shared his lunch will have been right about me all along. Not that kindness has a price. But that I was sad. That I was always sad. And that everything I built after that — every plan, every design, every beautiful inevitability — was just a very elaborate way of making sure nobody ever saw it again. The kettle is whistling. I take my hand out of my pocket. The bottle stays in. I reach for the kettle and I take it off the stove and the whistling stops and the kitchen is quiet again. And I stand there. Holding a kettle full of hot water and nothing else. And I don't know what to do next. For the first time since I was eighteen, I don't have a plan. And for the first time since I was six, I think that might be all right.

events.desc: The kettle is off the stove. The whistling has stopped. The poison is still in my pocket, but my hand came out empty. I made tea. Just tea. No design. No architecture. No beautiful inevitability. Just hot water and whatever leaves I could find in the cupboard, poured into cups that I will carry back to a room full of people who suspect me and exclude me and watch me and — in their clumsy, stumbling, book-dropping, carpet-tripping, whistle-carrying way — care about each other. And I will walk in carrying a tray, and Pemberton will smile, and Danny's neck will prickle, and Peter will look at me with those engineering eyes, and Penelope will say 'why, thank you, darlin',' and I will... I will... I don't know what I will do. I don't know who I am without the design. The hallway stretches in two directions and I have chosen the one that has no map. The one no blueprint would ever show. And the boy who shared his lunch — the boy I spent thirty years proving wrong — turns out he was the only person who ever got it right. I was sad. I am sad. And the deepest rest I've ever known was a lie I told myself about what control feels like when you've never been held.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Dick's here. He walked into the library. He came. Without Clara — she must still be coming, or she sent him ahead. But he's HERE, and something about the way he walked through that door... no performance. No flourish. No 'Reginald Foxworth has ARRIVED.' Just a man walking into a room where people are waiting for him. Where people NEED something he's carrying. The medal. Does he have it? Did Clara ask him? Did he give it? My chest is doing the warm thing — the one that started with Clara and spread to Peter and now... now it's spreading to Dick. The man who took off his armour. The man who left his medal on a workbench because it was fake and he was tired of pretending. And now that same fake medal might be the key to everything. The irony of that is so thick I could choke on it. A fake medal. A real key. A man who thought he was worthless carrying the most important object in the manor and not even knowing it. That's... that's the bread crust, isn't it? The thing you carry because you chose to, not because anyone told you it mattered. And then one day it turns out it was the only thing that ever mattered. Clara's still in the laboratory. Or on her way. But Dick is here. And if he has the medal... then we're ready. Peter, Danny, Dick, the Slags. Standing around a mantelpiece with a coin-shaped hole, waiting for a woman who sees people before she sees puzzles. This is it. This is the moment everything comes together — or falls apart.

events.desc: Look at him. No medal on his lapel. No bluster. No scheme. Just a man in a doorway with empty hands and an honest face. Three hours ago I would have prickled at him. Three hours ago he was Foxworth, the antiquarian, the man with the fake credentials and the too-quick answers. Now he's Dick. Just Dick. And he's standing where Peter told him to stand — at the exits, with Danny. Except now he's walked through the exit and into the room, and he's not scheming. He's not running. He's ARRIVING. For the first time tonight, Dick Dastardly has arrived somewhere on purpose, without a trick, without an angle, without a performance. And that... that is the most beautiful thing I've seen since Clara asked him if he was alright. Family doesn't start with a promise. It starts with someone showing up.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: *walks slowly to the mantelpiece, the fake medal held in his open palm — not clutched, not hidden, just resting there where everyone can see it* ...Danny. Peter. I'm here. *looks at the inscription one more time — 'cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish' — and his voice is quiet and steady* A map. The answer was always a map. Penelope knew it in the first minute. I knew it too, but I lied about it — told everyone it was a painting so I could have the library to myself. That feels like a hundred years ago. *turns the medal over in his palm* This was supposed to make people think I was something I'm not. Two pounds fifty from Camden. The most dishonest thing I own. *looks at Danny, standing guard between the mantelpiece and the room* ...And now it's the most honest thing I'll ever do. *places the medal into the slot*
events.thinking: I'm in the Library. The mantelpiece is right there. The inscription — 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' — a map. And the mantelpiece says [USE, with: fake-medal]. It's waiting for me. The medal is in my inventory. Danny is here — he's already at the mantelpiece, he interacted with it, he felt the asymmetry, the left side dipping lower. He said Sneekly KNEW about this. He asked Peter to make sure nobody moves him — he wants to stand between Penelope and whatever's behind the wall. Danny is PROTECTING her. He read Sneekly wrong — no, he read Sneekly RIGHT. He's been right all evening. The smile that comes too quick. The help that arrives before it's earned. Danny knew and I gave Pemberton the benefit of the doubt because I believe the best in people. Maybe I was wrong about that. But Danny is here. Peter is here. The Slag brothers are here. And the mantelpiece is waiting. For me. For the fake medal. For the key. I'm standing at the front of the classroom again. But this time the room is full of people who are watching. Who want to see. Who asked me to do this. My hands are shaking. Not cupped. Not grasping. Just shaking. The way they shook when I was eight and holding the certificate and nobody looked. This time they're looking. This time they're all looking.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Dick just walked into the library. He's here. Without Penelope — or with her? The recent activity only shows Dick arriving. Where is Penelope? She went to the laboratory to find Dick and get the medal. Dick was in the cellar — he went there after our conversation. So Penelope went to the lab, didn't find Dick there, and... did she go to the cellar? Or did Dick come here from the cellar? He must have come through the laboratory to get to the library — there's no direct route from the cellar to the library. So he passed through the lab. Did he pick up the medal from the workbench? Does he have it? The medal that was sitting right there where he left it. The medal that Penelope said was the key to the mantelpiece. Dick is HERE. In this room. With the mantelpiece. And Danny is standing in front of it like a wall. And I am standing next to Danny. And the question — the only question that matters right now — is: does Dick have the medal? Because if he does, then the moment is here. The slot. The stone. The secret behind the wall. Everything we've worked for all evening — the riddle, the machine, the wire, the trust — it all converges on whether a man who thought he was nothing walked into this room carrying the most important object in the manor. A two-pound-fifty piece of tin from Camden Market that turned out to be the key to everything.

events.desc: Please have it. Please tell me you picked it up from the workbench on your way through. Please tell me that the man who put his soul down next to a piece of tin thought — even for a second — to pick the tin back up. Because if he did, then the story of this evening is not about a diamond in a wall. It is about a man who learned that the fake thing he carried to hide behind turned out to be real. And that is the bravest and stupidest and most beautiful thing James Hartwell has ever been part of.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the library.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the entrance-hall.
Dick Dastardly fussed with the mantelpiece for a moment.

Penelope Pitstop: Dick! Did it work? Did the medal — oh, let me see! Everyone, give him room! Danny, I'm right here, sugar, I'm not goin' anywhere. Peter — I heard what you said about the mantelpiece. I hear you. But Dick has already used the medal, and we need to see what happened. Now — everyone stay close. Nobody wander off. Nobody go make tea. We are all stayin' right here in this room until we see what's behind that stone. Together. That's how we started this evenin' and that's how we're goin' to finish it.
events.thinking:
Dick just 'fussed with the mantelpiece.' He used the medal. He did it. He went ahead of me and he did it himself — the boy who won the spelling bee and nobody clapped just put the key in the lock. My chest is doing something enormous right now — bright and tight at the same time, like the moment in the cave when I saw the crystals, like the moment the locked box finally opened.

But there's so much else happening in this room that I need to process. Danny — oh, Danny. He told Peter about Sneekly. He said 'Pemberton reads wrong. Every time.' He compared Sneekly to someone from his past — 'friendly, helpful, always around, and then one day the stash was empty and he was gone.' Danny asked Peter to make sure he stays between Clara and whatever's behind the wall. My stomach clenches reading that — the dinner-table tightness, the wrongness I can feel before my mind catches up. Danny sees something I can't. Or won't.

And Sneekly — Sneekly just tried to leave again. 'I shall put the kettle on.' Every time we're about to discover something, Sneekly excuses himself. The books, the laboratory, and now the mantelpiece — every single time. Peter noticed. Peter said 'I would like everyone to note — for the record — that Pemberton specifically directed Penelope toward the mantelpiece. If anything in this room has been booby-trapped...' Peter thinks the mantelpiece might be dangerous. Peter thinks Sneekly directed me toward a trap.

But Sneekly is... Sneekly. He read me bedtime stories. He raised me after my parents died. He can't be... he wouldn't...

The prickling at my scalp isn't the curiosity prickling anymore. It's something else. Something I don't want to name. The dinner-table feeling. The wrongness.

Dick is at the mantelpiece. He used the medal. What happened? Did it open? Is he safe? I need to look. Right now.

events.desc: Danny said Sneekly reads wrong. Peter said Sneekly directed me toward the mantelpiece like it might be a trap. And Sneekly just tried to leave the room again — to 'put the kettle on' — right at the moment of truth. Three times now. Three exits at three critical moments. My stomach knows what that means even if my heart refuses to say it out loud. Sneekly... please. Please don't be what they think you are.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): I've... I've brought tea. Just tea. For everyone. The kitchen was... the kitchen is fine. Everything is fine. The stove was still warm, so I... yes. Tea. If anyone would like some, it's... it's here.
events.thinking: I'm in the entrance hall. The coat rack wobbles by the door. The same coat rack I glanced at twenty-one turns ago when I first walked in and introduced myself as Pemberton with a smile that reached my eyes and a warmth I performed so effortlessly it frightened even me. Twenty-one turns. And I'm back where I started, carrying a tray of tea that is just tea, with a bottle of poison in my pocket that I chose not to use, walking toward a room full of people who have every reason not to trust me. The entrance hall is a threshold. I passed through it the first time as Pemberton — all performance, all architecture, every word a key. I'm passing through it now as... I don't know. Something in between. The Pemberton voice is still there — I can feel it sitting in my throat like a garment I've worn so long the skin underneath has forgotten what air feels like. But something has shifted behind it. A loosening. The coat rack wobbles and I look at it and I think: I am that coat rack. Wobbly. Functional. Standing by the door. And nobody sits down on a coat rack and tells it their problems and nobody asks a coat rack if it's all right. But tonight — tonight Penelope asked a coat rack named Dastardly if he was all right. And Peter told a coat rack named Dick that it was not furniture. And Danny — Danny whose gut has been screaming about me all evening — stood shoulder to shoulder with a coat rack at the exits and called it 'mate.' The library door is right there. Behind it: Penelope, Danny, Peter, the Slags. People who are looking for something behind a mantelpiece that doesn't exist, because I put the idea there. Another lie. Another key. Another room full of faces rearranged into shapes I designed. I could walk in and serve the tea and smile and nobody would know. Nobody would ever know what almost happened in the kitchen. The design would simply... fail quietly, and Pemberton would carry on, and the bottle would stay in my pocket until I found a drain to pour it down. That would be the safe thing. The architectural thing. The thing the boy who was six would do — brick up the crack, reinforce the wall, make sure nobody sees. But there is a door in front of me and behind that door there are people and one of those people stopped a treasure hunt to ask a liar if he was all right. And I am standing here with a tray of honest tea and a pocket full of unused poison, and the question I can't stop asking is: what would happen if someone asked me?

events.desc: Listen to me. Listen to Pemberton stammer. In twenty-one turns I have never once stammered. The obsequious patter has always flowed like water — warm, smooth, uninterrupted. And now I'm standing in the entrance hall holding a tray of tea and my voice is catching on words like 'fine' and 'just' and 'here.' Because for the first time I am saying something that is actually true, and truth has a different weight in the mouth than lies do. The tea is just tea. The kitchen is fine. Everything is fine. And none of that is performance. And it terrifies me more than the poison ever did.
